**Édouard Louis Joseph, [Baron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baron "Baron") Merckx** (born 17 June 1945), is a Belgian former professional road and track cyclist racer who is the most successful rider in the history of competitive cycling. His victories include an unequalled eleven [Grand Tours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Tour_(cycling) "Grand Tour (cycling)") (five [Tours de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tour_de_France "Tour de France"), five [Giros d'Italia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giro_d'Italia "Giro d'Italia"), and a [Vuelta a España](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vuelta_a_Espa%C3%B1a "Vuelta a España")), all five [Monuments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument "Cycling monument"), setting the [hour record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hour_record "Hour record"), three [World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UCI_Road_World_Championships "UCI Road World Championships"), every major one-day race other than [Paris–Tours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris%E2%80%93Tours "Paris–Tours"), and extensive victories on the track.

Born in [Meensel-Kiezegem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meensel-Kiezegem "Meensel-Kiezegem"), [Brabant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Province_of_Brabant "Province of Brabant"), Belgium, he grew up in [Woluwe-Saint-Pierre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woluwe-Saint-Pierre "Woluwe-Saint-Pierre") where his parents ran a grocery store. He played several sports, but found his true passion in cycling. Merckx got his first bicycle at the age of three or four and competed in his first race in 1961. His first victory came at [Petit-Enghien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petit-Enghien "Petit-Enghien") in October 1961.

After winning 80 races as an amateur, he turned professional on 29 April 1965 when he signed with [Solo–Superia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solo%E2%80%93Superia "Solo–Superia"). His first major victory came in the [Milan–San Remo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milan%E2%80%93San_Remo "Milan–San Remo") a year later, after switching to [Peugeot–BP–Michelin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peugeot_(cycling_team) "Peugeot (cycling team)"). After the 1967 season, Merckx moved to [Faema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faemino%E2%80%93Faema "Faemino–Faema"), and won the [Giro d'Italia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1968_Giro_d'Italia "1968 Giro d'Italia"), his first Grand Tour victory. Four times between 1970 and 1974, Merckx completed a Grand Tour double. His final double also coincided with winning the elite [men's road race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_UCI_Road_World_Championships_%E2%80%93_Men's_road_race "1974 UCI Road World Championships – Men's road race") at the [UCI Road World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_UCI_Road_World_Championships "1974 UCI Road World Championships") to make him the first rider to accomplish cycling's [Triple Crown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple_Crown_of_Cycling "Triple Crown of Cycling"). Merckx broke the hour record in October 1972, extending the record by almost 800 metres.

He acquired the nickname "**the Cannibal**", suggested by the daughter of a teammate upon being told by her father of how Merckx would not let anyone else win. Merckx achieved 525 victories over his eighteen-year career. He is one of only three riders to have won all five '[Monuments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_monument "Cycling monument")' ([Milan–San Remo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milan%E2%80%93San_Remo "Milan–San Remo"), [Tour of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tour_of_Flanders_(men's_race) "Tour of Flanders (men's race)"), [Paris–Roubaix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris%E2%80%93Roubaix "Paris–Roubaix"), [Liège–Bastogne–Liège](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li%C3%A8ge%E2%80%93Bastogne%E2%80%93Li%C3%A8ge "Liège–Bastogne–Liège"), and the [Giro di Lombardia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giro_di_Lombardia "Giro di Lombardia")) and the only one to have won them all at least twice. Merckx was successful on the road and also on the track, as well as in the large stage races and one-day races. He is almost universally regarded as the greatest and most successful rider in the history of cycling.

Since Merckx's retirement from the sport on 18 May 1978, he has remained active in the cycling world. He began his own bicycle brand, [Eddy Merckx Cycles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx_Cycles "Eddy Merckx Cycles"), in 1980 and its bicycles were used by several professional teams in the 1980s, 1990s and early 2000s. Merckx coached the Belgian national cycling team for eleven years, stopping in 1996. He helped start and organize the [Tour of Qatar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tour_of_Qatar "Tour of Qatar") from its start in 2002 until its final edition in 2016. He also assisted in running the [Tour of Oman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tour_of_Oman "Tour of Oman"), before a disagreement with the organizers led him to step away in 2017.

## Early life and amateur career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Eddy_Merckx&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and amateur career")]

Édouard Louis Joseph Merckx was born in [Meensel-Kiezegem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meensel-Kiezegem "Meensel-Kiezegem"),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-VN_EM_70-3)[Brabant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Province_of_Brabant "Province of Brabant"), [Belgium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgium "Belgium"), on 17 June 1945 to Jules Merckx and Jenny Pittomvils.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFriebe2012104-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201220-5) Merckx was the first-born of the family.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFriebe2012104-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201220-5) In September 1946, the family moved to [Sint-Pieters-Woluwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woluwe-Saint-Pierre "Woluwe-Saint-Pierre"), in [Brussels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brussels "Brussels"), Belgium, in order to take over a grocery shop that had been up for lease.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201222-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-Guard_Review-7) In May 1948, Jenny gave birth to twins: a boy, Michel, and a girl, Micheline.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201223-8) As a child Eddy was hyperactive and was always playing outside.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201223%E2%80%9324-9)

Eddy was a competitive child and played several sports, including [basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball "Basketball"), [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football"), [table tennis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Table_tennis "Table tennis") and [boxing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boxing "Boxing"), the latter in which he won some local boxing tournaments.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201224-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201225-11) He even played lawn tennis for the local junior team.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201225-11) However, Merckx claimed he knew he wanted to be a cyclist at the age of four and that his first memory was a crash on his bike when he was the same age.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-G_H-12) Merckx began riding a bike at the age of three or four and would ride to school every day, beginning at age eight.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201230-13) Merckx would imitate his cycling idol [Stan Ockers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Ockers "Stan Ockers") with his friends when they rode bikes together.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201228%E2%80%9329-14)

In summer 1961, Merckx bought his first racing license and competed in his first official race a month after he turned sixteen, coming in sixth place.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201231-15) He rode in twelve more races before winning his first, at [Petit-Enghien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petit-Enghien "Petit-Enghien"), on 1 October 1961.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201315%E2%80%9316-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFriebe2012108-17)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-VN_EM_70-3) In the winter following his first victory, he trained with former racer [Félicien Vervaecke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F%C3%A9licien_Vervaecke "Félicien Vervaecke") at the local [velodrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velodrome "Velodrome").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201232-18) Merckx won his second victory on 11 March 1962 in a [kermis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kermesse_(cycling) "Kermesse (cycling)") race.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201232-18) Merckx competed in 55 races during the 1962 calendar year; as he devoted more time to cycling, his grades at school began to decline.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFriebe2012108%E2%80%93109-19) After winning the Belgian amateur road race title, Merckx declined an offer from his school's headmaster to have his exams postponed, and dropped out of school.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFriebe2012109%E2%80%93110-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-EN_H-21) He finished the season with 23 victories to his name.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-EN_H-21)

Merckx won the [amateur road race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UCI_Road_World_Championships_%E2%80%93_Men's_amateur_road_race "UCI Road World Championships – Men's amateur road race") at the [1964 UCI Road World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_UCI_Road_World_Championships "1964 UCI Road World Championships") in [Sallanches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sallanches "Sallanches"), France.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHeijmansMallon2011131-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-LS_WARR-23) The following month, he came twelfth in [the individual road race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_at_the_1964_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_individual_road_race "Cycling at the 1964 Summer Olympics – Men's individual road race") at the [Tokyo Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_Summer_Olympics "1964 Summer Olympics").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-CDS_64_ORR-24)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-sports-reference-2) Merckx remained an amateur until April 1965, and finished his amateur career with eighty wins to his credit.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-VN_60-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-L'%C3%89quipe_13_March_2007-26)

## Professional career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Eddy_Merckx&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Professional career")]

### 1965–1967: Solo–Superia and Peugeot–BP–Michelin

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Eddy_Merckx&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1965–1967: Solo–Superia and Peugeot–BP–Michelin")]

#### 1965: First professional season

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Eddy_Merckx&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 1965: First professional season")]

Merckx turned professional on 29 April 1965 when he signed with [Rik Van Looy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rik_Van_Looy "Rik Van Looy")'s Belgian team, [Solo–Superia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solo%E2%80%93Superia "Solo–Superia").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFriebe201217-27) He won his first race in [Vilvoorde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vilvoorde "Vilvoorde"), beating [Emile Daems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emile_Daems "Emile Daems").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFriebe201219-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201349-29) On 1 August,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFriebe201219-28) Merckx finished second in the Belgian national championships, which qualified him for the [men's road race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1965_UCI_Road_World_Championships_%E2%80%93_Men's_road_race "1965 UCI Road World Championships – Men's road race") at the [UCI Road World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1965_UCI_Road_World_Championships "1965 UCI Road World Championships").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-CW_Int-30)[Raphaël Géminiani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapha%C3%ABl_G%C3%A9miniani "Raphaël Géminiani"), the manager of the Bic cycling team, approached Merckx at the event and offered him 2,500 francs a month to join the team the following season.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201350-31) Merckx chose to sign; however, since he was a minor the contract was invalid.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201350-31)

After finishing the road race in 29th position,[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-32) Merckx returned to Belgium and discussed his plans for the next season with his manager [Jean Van Buggenhout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Van_Buggenhout "Jean Van Buggenhout").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201350-31) Van Buggenhout helped orchestrate a move that sent Merckx to the French-based [Peugeot–BP–Michelin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peugeot%E2%80%93BP%E2%80%93Michelin "Peugeot–BP–Michelin") for 20,000 francs a month.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201350-31) Merckx elected to leave Solo–Superia due to the way he was treated by his teammates, in particular Van Looy.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-CW_Int-30) Van Looy and other teammates mocked Merckx for his various habits such as his eating, or called him names.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFriebe201220-33) In addition, Merckx later stated that during his time with Van Looy's team he had not been taught anything.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201349-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-CW_Int-30) While with Solo–Superia, he won nine races out of the nearly 70 races he entered.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201350-31)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201353-34)

#### 1966: First Monument victory

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Eddy_Merckx&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 1966: First Monument victory")]

[![Image 16: A man on a bicycle, with a car behind him.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/10/Eddy_Merckx_1966.jpg/250px-Eddy_Merckx_1966.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Eddy_Merckx_1966.jpg)

Merckx finished in twelfth position in the men's road race at the [1966 UCI Road World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_UCI_Road_World_Championships "1966 UCI Road World Championships")

In March 1966, Merckx entered his first major stage race as a professional rider, the [Paris–Nice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris%E2%80%93Nice "Paris–Nice").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201351-35) He took the race lead for a single stage before losing it to [Jacques Anquetil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Anquetil "Jacques Anquetil") and eventually coming in fourth overall.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201351-35)[Milan–San Remo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milan%E2%80%93San_Remo "Milan–San Remo"), his first participation in one of cycling's Monuments, was the next event on the calendar for Merckx. There, he succeeded in staying with the main field as the race entered the final climb of the [Poggio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poggio_di_San_Remo "Poggio di San Remo").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201352-36) He attacked on the climb and reduced the field to a group of eleven, himself included.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201351%E2%80%9352-37) Merckx was advised by his manager to hold off on sprinting full-out to the finish line until as late as possible.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201352-36) At the end of the race, three other riders approached the line with him, and Merckx beat them in the sprint.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201352-36) In the following weeks, he raced the [Tour of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tour_of_Flanders_(men's_race) "Tour of Flanders (men's race)") and [Paris–Roubaix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris%E2%80%93Roubaix "Paris–Roubaix"), the most important [cobbled classics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cobbled_classics "Cobbled classics"); in the former he crashed and in the latter he had a punctured tire.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201357-38) At the [1966 UCI Road World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_UCI_Road_World_Championships "1966 UCI Road World Championships") he finished twelfth in the road race after suffering a cramp in the closing kilometers.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201357-38) He finished the 1966 season with a total of 20 wins, including his first stage race win at the Tour of Morbihan.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201357-38)

#### 1967: Second straight Milan–San Remo and world champion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Eddy_Merckx&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 1967: Second straight Milan–San Remo and world champion")]

Merckx opened the 1967 campaign with two stage victories at the [Giro di Sardegna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giro_di_Sardegna "Giro di Sardegna").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201358-39) He followed these successes by entering [Paris–Nice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_Paris%E2%80%93Nice "1967 Paris–Nice") where he won the second stage and took the race lead.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201358-39) Two stages later, a teammate, [Tom Simpson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Simpson "Tom Simpson"), attacked with several other riders on a climb and was nearly 20 minutes ahead of Merckx, who remained in a group behind.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201358-39) Merckx attacked two days later on a climb 70 km into the stage.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201359-40) He was able to establish a firm advantage, but obeyed orders from his manager to wait for the chasing Simpson.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201359-40) Merckx won the stage, while Simpson secured his overall victory.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201359-40)

[![Image 17: Eddy Merckx being pushed while on bike before a stage.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/Eddy_Merckx_1967.jpg/250px-Eddy_Merckx_1967.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Eddy_Merckx_1967.jpg)

At the [1967 Giro d'Italia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_Giro_d'Italia "1967 Giro d'Italia") Merckx won his first [Grand Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Tour_(cycling) "Grand Tour (cycling)") stages on the way to finishing ninth overall

On 18 March,[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-CDS_67_MSR-41) Merckx started the [Milan–San Remo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_Milan%E2%80%93San_Remo "1967 Milan–San Remo") and was seen as a 120–1 favorite to win the race.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201359-40) He attacked on the Capo Berta and again on the Poggio, leaving only Gianni Motta with him.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201360-42) The two slowed their pace and were joined by two more riders.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201360-42) Merckx won the four-man sprint to the finish.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201360-42) His next victory came in [La Flèche Wallonne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Fl%C3%A8che_Wallonne "La Flèche Wallonne") after he missed out on an early break, caught up to it, and attacked from it to win the race.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201362-43) On 20 May, he started the [Giro d'Italia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_Giro_d'Italia "1967 Giro d'Italia"), his first [Grand Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Tour_(cycling) "Grand Tour (cycling)").[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201364-44) He won the twelfth and fourteenth stages en route to finishing ninth in the general classification.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-BRI_1967-45)

He signed with [Faema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faemino%E2%80%93Faema "Faemino–Faema") on 2 September for ten years worth 400,000 Belgian francs.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201365-46) He chose to switch over in order to be in complete control over the team he was racing for.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201365-46) In addition, he would not have to pay for various expenses that came with racing such as wheels and tires.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201366-47) The next day, Merckx started the men's road race at the [1967 UCI Road World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_UCI_Road_World_Championships "1967 UCI Road World Championships") in [Heerlen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heerlen "Heerlen"), Netherlands.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201368-48) The course consisted of ten laps of a circuit.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201366-47) Motta attacked on the first lap and was joined by Merckx and five other riders.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201368-48) The group thinned to five as they reached the finish line where Merckx was able to out-sprint [Jan Janssen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Janssen "Jan Janssen") for first place.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201368-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-ELM_67_WC-49) In doing so, he became the third rider to win the world road race amateur and professional titles.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201368-48) By winning the race he earned the right to wear the [rainbow jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow_jersey "Rainbow jersey") as world champion.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201368-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-ELM_67_WC-49)

### 1968–1970: Faema

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Eddy_Merckx&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 1968–1970: Faema")]

#### 1968: First Grand Tour victory

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Eddy_Merckx&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 1968: First Grand Tour victory")]

Merckx's first victory with his new team came in a stage win at the Giro di Sardegna.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201371-50) At Paris–Nice, he was forced to quit the race due to a knee injury he sustained during the event.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201372-51) He failed to win his third consecutive Milan–San Remo and missed out at the Tour of Flanders the following weekend.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201372-51) His next victory came at Paris–Roubaix when he bested [Herman Van Springel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herman_Van_Springel "Herman Van Springel") in a race that was plagued by poor weather and several punctures to the competing riders.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201372-51) At the behest of his team, Merckx raced the [Giro d'Italia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1968_Giro_d'Italia "1968 Giro d'Italia") instead of the [Tour de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1968_Tour_de_France "1968 Tour de France").[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201372-51) He won the race's second stage after he attacked with one kilometer to go.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201372%E2%80%9373-52)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-BRI_1968_G-53) The twelfth stage was marred by rainy weather and featured the climbs of the [Tre Cime di Lavaredo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tre_Cime_di_Lavaredo "Tre Cime di Lavaredo") for the stage finish.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-BRI_1968_G-53) By the time Merckx had reached the penultimate climb, there was a six-man group at the front of the race with a nine-minute advantage.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201373-54) Merckx attacked and was able to get a sizable distance between himself and the group he left before he stopped to change his wheel in order to slow down due to orders from his team manager.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-BRI_1968_G-53)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201374-55) Merckx got back on his bike and caught the leading breakaway and rode past it to the finish, where he won the stage and took the race lead.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-BRI_1968_G-53)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201375-56) Merckx went on to win the race, along with the [points classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Points_classification_in_the_Giro_d'Italia "Points classification in the Giro d'Italia") and [mountains classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountains_classification_in_the_Giro_d'Italia "Mountains classification in the Giro d'Italia").[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-BRI_1968_G-53) In the [Volta a Catalunya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volta_a_Catalunya "Volta a Catalunya"), Merckx took the race lead from Gimondi in the race's time trial stage and won the event as a whole.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201376%E2%80%9377-57) He finished the season with 32 wins in the 129 races he entered.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013293-58)

#### 1969: A victory in Paris and injury in Blois

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Eddy_Merckx&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: 1969: A victory in Paris and injury in Blois")]

Merckx opened the 1969 season with victories at the [Vuelta a Levante](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volta_a_la_Comunitat_Valenciana "Volta a la Comunitat Valenciana") and the Paris–Nice overall, as well as stages in each of the races.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201388-59) On 30 March 1969 Merckx earned his first major victory of the 1969 calendar with his win at the [Tour of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1969_Tour_of_Flanders "1969 Tour of Flanders").[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201386-60) On a rainy day that featured strong winds,[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201386-60) he attacked first on the Oude Kwaremont, but a puncture nullified any gains he was able to establish.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201387-61) He made a move on the Kapelmuur and was followed by a few riders.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201387-61) As the wind shifted from a crosswind to a headwind with close to seventy kilometers left to go, Merckx increased the pace and rode solo to victory.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201387-61) The 17 days after the Tour of Flanders saw Merckx win nine times.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201388-59) He won Milan–San Remo by descending the Poggio at high speed.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201388-59) Merckx saw victory again in mid-April at the [Liège–Bastogne–Liège](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1969_Li%C3%A8ge%E2%80%93Bastogne%E2%80%93Li%C3%A8ge "1969 Liège–Bastogne–Liège") when he attacked with 70 kilometers remaining.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham201389-62)

He began the [Giro d'Italia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1969_Giro_d'Italia "1969 Giro d'Italia") on 16 May, stating that he wished to ride less aggressively than the year before in order to save energy for the [Tour de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1969_Tour_de_France "1969 Tour de France").[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013100%E2%80%93101-63) Merckx had won four of the race's stages and held the race lead going into the sixteenth day of racing.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013101-64) However, before the start of the stage race director Vincenzo Torriani, along with a television camera and two writers, entered Merckx's hotel room and informed him that he had failed a doping control and was disqualified from the race, in addition to being suspended for a month.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013101%E2%80%93102-65) On 14 June, the cycling governing body, the FICP, overturned the month long suspension and cleared him due to the "benefit of the doubt."[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013107-66)

[![Image 18: A green field with the words "Coupe du monde".](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/8/84/Mourenx_velodrome_003.JPG/250px-Mourenx_velodrome_003.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mourenx_velodrome_003.JPG)

The Velodrome Eddy Merckx at Mourenx was named in honor of Merckx in 1999 due to his efforts during the seventeenth stage at the [1969 Tour de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1969_Tour_de_France "1969 Tour de France")

Before starting the Tour, Merckx had spent a large amount of his time resting and training, racing only five times.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013110-67) Merckx won the race's sixth stage through attacking before the leg's final major climb, the Ballon d'Alsace, and then outlasting his competitors who were able to follow him initially.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013119%E2%80%93120-68) During the seventeenth stage, Merckx was riding at the head of the race with several general classification contenders on the [Col du Tourmalet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Col_du_Tourmalet "Col du Tourmalet").[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013112-69) Merckx shifted into a large gear, attacked, and went on to cross the summit with a 45-second advantage.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013112%E2%80%93113-70) Despite orders to wait for the chasing riders, Merckx increased his efforts.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013113-71) He rode over the [Col du Soulor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Col_du_Soulor "Col du Soulor") and [Col d'Aubisque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Col_d'Aubisque "Col d'Aubisque"), increasing the gap to eight minutes.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013113-71) With close to fifty kilometers to go, Merckx began to suffer [hypoglycemia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypoglycemia "Hypoglycemia") and rode the rest of the stage in severe pain.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013114-72) At the end of the stage, Merckx told the journalists "I hope I have done enough now for you to consider me a worthy winner."[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013114-72) Merckx finished the race with six stage victories to his credit, along with the general, points, mountains, and combination classifications, and the award for most aggressive rider.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013123-73)

His next major race was the two-day race, [Paris–Luxembourg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris%E2%80%93Luxembourg "Paris–Luxembourg").[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013128-74) Merckx was down fifty-four seconds going into the second day and attacked eight kilometers from the finish, on the slopes of the Bereldange.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013128-74) Merckx rode solo to catch the leading rider Jacques Anquetil, whom he dropped with a kilometer remaining.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013128%E2%80%93129-75) Merckx won the stage and gained enough time on the race leader Gimondi to win the race.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013129-76)

[![Image 19: An illustration of a derny.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bc/Derny.jpg/250px-Derny.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Derny.jpg)

Fernand Wambst, who was regarded as a great [derny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derny "Derny") driver, agreed to pace Merckx in the omnium events in [Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blois "Blois")[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013134-77)

On 9 September, Merckx participated in a three-round [omnium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omnium "Omnium") event at the concrete velodrome in [Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blois "Blois") where each rider was to be paced by a [derny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derny "Derny").[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013133-78)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013134-77) Fernand Wambst was Merckx's pacer for the contest.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013134-77) After winning the first intermediate sprint of the first round, Wambst chose to slow their pace and move to the back of the race despite Merckx wanting to stay out in front for fear of an accident.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013135-79) Wambst wanted to pass everyone to provide a show for the crowd.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013135-79) The duo then increased their pace and began to pass each of the other contestants;[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013135-79) however, as they passed the riders in first position, the leading derny lost control and crashed into the wall.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013135-79) Wambst chose to avoid the derny by going below it, but the leader's derny came back down and collided with Wambst, while Merckx's pedal caught one of the dernies.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013136-80) The two riders landed head first onto the track.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013136-80)

> ‘’Blois was the worst experience of my career. Here I could have been dead. The accident cost me a few years of my career, because afterwards, with that back, I never had the same feeling uphill as I had in that very first Tour of ‘69.’'

—Eddy Merckx in 2005[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-81)

Wambst died of a fractured skull as he was being transported to a hospital.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013136-80) Merckx remained unconscious for 45 minutes and awoke in the operating room.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013136-80) He sustained a [concussion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concussion "Concussion"), [whiplash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whiplash_(medicine) "Whiplash (medicine)"), trapped nerves in his back, a displaced [pelvis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelvis "Pelvis"), and several other cuts and bruises.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013137-82) He remained at the hospital for a week before returning to Belgium.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013137-82) He spent six weeks in bed before beginning to race again in October.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013137-82) Merckx later stated that he "was never the same again" after the crash.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013137-82)[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-BRI_1970_Giro-83) He would constantly adjust the height of his seat during races to help ease the pain.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013138-84)

#### 1970: A Giro–Tour double

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Eddy_Merckx&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: 1970: A Giro–Tour double")]

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/92/Eddy_Merckx-1970-Panini.jpg/250px-Eddy_Merckx-1970-Panini.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Eddy_Merckx-1970-Panini.jpg)

Merckx with [Faemino–Faema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faemino%E2%80%93Faema "Faemino–Faema") in 1970

Merckx entered the 1970 campaign nursing a case of mild [tendonitis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tendonitis "Tendonitis") in his [knee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knee "Knee").[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013140-85) His first major victory came in Paris–Nice where he won the general classification, along with three stages.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013140-85)[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-BRI_1970_Giro-83) On 1 April, Merckx won the [Gent–Wevelgem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gent%E2%80%93Wevelgem "Gent–Wevelgem"), followed by the [Tour of Belgium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tour_of_Belgium "Tour of Belgium") – where he braved a snowy stage and followed the day up with a victory in the final time trial to secure the title – and [Paris–Roubaix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1970_Paris%E2%80%93Roubaix "1970 Paris–Roubaix").[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013140%E2%80%93141-86)[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-BRI_1970_Giro-83) In Paris–Roubaix, Merckx was battling a cold as the race began in heavy rain.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013140-85) He attacked thirty-one kilometers from the finish and went on to win by five minutes and twenty-one seconds, the largest margin of victory in the history of the race.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013140-85) The next weekend, Merckx attempted to race for teammate [Joseph Bruyère](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Bruy%C3%A8re "Joseph Bruyère") in La Flèche Wallonne; however, Bruyère was unable to keep pace with the leading riders, leaving Merckx to take the victory.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013141-87)

[![Image 21: The summit of a mountain.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/96/Ventoux_Flamme_Rouge_%2814829387042%29.jpg/250px-Ventoux_Flamme_Rouge_%2814829387042%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ventoux_Flamme_Rouge_(14829387042).jpg)

After winning the fourteenth stage to the summit of [Mont Ventoux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mont_Ventoux "Mont Ventoux") during the [1970 Tour de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1970_Tour_de_France "1970 Tour de France"), Merckx had to be given oxygen

After the scandal at the previous year's Giro d'Italia, Merckx was unwilling to return to the race in [1970](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1970_Giro_d'Italia "1970 Giro d'Italia").[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013141-87) His entry to the race was contingent upon all doping controls being sent to a lab in Rome to be tested, rather than being tested at the finish like the year before.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013141-87) He started the race and won the second stage,[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-BRI_1970_Giro-83) but four days later showed signs of weakness with his knee as he was dropped twice while in the mountains.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013141-87) However the next day, Merckx attacked on the final climb into the city of [Brentonico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brentonico "Brentonico") to win the stage and take the lead.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-BRI_1970_Giro-83) He won the stage nine [individual time trial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Individual_time_trial "Individual time trial") by almost two minutes over the second-place finisher, expanding his lead significantly.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-BRI_1970_Giro-83) Merckx did not win another stage, but expanded his lead a little more before the race's conclusion.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-BRI_1970_Giro-83)

Before beginning the Tour, Merckx won the men's road race at the [Belgian National Road Race Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgian_National_Road_Race_Championships "Belgian National Road Race Championships").[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-BRI_1970_Tour-88) Merckx won the [Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1970_Tour_de_France "1970 Tour de France")'s opening prologue to take the race's first race leader's [yellow jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_classification_in_the_Tour_de_France "General classification in the Tour de France").[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-BRI_1970_Tour-88)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013142-89) After losing the lead following the second stage,[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-BRI_1970_Tour-88)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013142-89) he won the sixth stage after forming a breakaway with [Lucien Van Impe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucien_Van_Impe "Lucien Van Impe") and regained the lead.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013143-90) After expanding his lead in the stage nine individual time trial, Merckx won the race's first true mountain stage, stage 10, and expanded his lead to five minutes in the general classification.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-BRI_1970_Tour-88)[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013143-90)

Merckx won three of the five stages contested within the next four days, including a summit finish to [Mont Ventoux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mont_Ventoux "Mont Ventoux"), where upon finishing he was given [oxygen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen "Oxygen").[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013143%E2%80%93144-91)[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013145-92) Merckx won two more stages, both individual time trials, and won the Tour by over twelve minutes. He finished the Tour with eight stage victories and won the mountains and combination classifications.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-BRI_1970_Tour-88)[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013145-92) The eight stage wins equaled the previous record for stage wins in a single Tour de France.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-BRI_1970_Tour-88)[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013146-93) Merckx also became the third to accomplish the feat of winning the Giro and Tour in the same calendar year.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-BRI_1970_Tour-88)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013142-89)

### 1971–1976: Molteni

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Eddy_Merckx&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: 1971–1976: Molteni")]

#### 1971: A third consecutive Tour and second world championship

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Eddy_Merckx&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: 1971: A third consecutive Tour and second world championship")]

[![Image 22: A picture of a cyclist in a jersey that reads "Bic."](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a2/Tour_de_France%2C_Luis_Oca%C3%B1a%2C_Bestanddeelnr_926-5233.jpg/250px-Tour_de_France%2C_Luis_Oca%C3%B1a%2C_Bestanddeelnr_926-5233.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tour_de_France,_Luis_Oca%C3%B1a,_Bestanddeelnr_926-5233.jpg)

Spaniard [Luis Ocaña](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luis_Oca%C3%B1a "Luis Ocaña") (pictured at the [1973 Tour de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_Tour_de_France "1973 Tour de France")) was one of Merckx's major rivals during the [1971 Tour de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1971_Tour_de_France "1971 Tour de France")

Faema folded at the end of the 1970 season causing Merckx and several of his teammates to move to another Italian team, [Molteni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molteni_(cycling_team) "Molteni (cycling team)").[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013162-94)[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFoot2011225-95) The first major victory for Merckx came in the Giro di Sardegna, which he secured after attacking on his own and riding solo through the rain to win the race's final stage.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013162-94) He followed that with his third consecutive Paris–Nice victory, a race he led from start to finish.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013162-94) In the Milan–San Remo, Merckx worked with his teammates in a seven-man breakaway to set up a final attack on the Poggio.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013162-94) Merckx's attack succeeded and he won his fourth edition of the race.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013162-94) Six days later, he won the [Omloop Het Volk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omloop_Het_Nieuwsblad "Omloop Het Nieuwsblad").[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013162-94)

After winning the Tour of Belgium again, Merckx headed into the major spring classics.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013163-96) During the Tour of Flanders, Merckx's rivals worked against him to prevent him from winning.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013163-96) A week later, he suffered five flat tires during the Paris–Roubaix.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013163-96) The [Liège–Bastogne–Liège](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1971_Li%C3%A8ge%E2%80%93Bastogne%E2%80%93Li%C3%A8ge "1971 Liège–Bastogne–Liège") was held in cold and rain conditions.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013163-96) After attacking ninety kilometers from the finish, Merckx caught the leaders on the road and passed them.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013163-96) He rode solo until around three kilometers to go when Georges Pintens caught him.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013163-96) Merckx and Pintens rode to the finish together, where Merckx won the two-man sprint.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013164-97) Instead of racing the Giro d'Italia, Merckx elected to enter two shorter stages races in France, the [Grand Prix du Midi Libre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Prix_du_Midi_Libre "Grand Prix du Midi Libre") and the [Critérium du Dauphiné](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crit%C3%A9rium_du_Dauphin%C3%A9 "Critérium du Dauphiné"), both of which he won.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013164-97)

The [Tour de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1971_Tour_de_France "1971 Tour de France") began with a [team time trial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Team_time_trial "Team time trial") that Merckx's team won, giving him the lead.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013165-98) The next day's racing was split into three parts.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013165-98) Merckx lost the lead after stage 1b, but regained it after stage 1c due to a time bonus that he earned from winning an intermediate sprint.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013165-98) During the second stage, a major break with the major race contenders, including Merckx, formed with over a hundred kilometers to go.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013166-99) The group finished nine minutes ahead of the peloton as Merckx came around [Roger De Vlaeminck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_De_Vlaeminck "Roger De Vlaeminck") during the sprint to win the day.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013166-99) After a week of racing, Merckx held a lead of around a minute over the main contenders.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013166-99) The eighth stage saw a mountain top finish to [Puy-de-Dôme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puy-de-D%C3%B4me "Puy-de-Dôme").[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013166-99)[Bernard Thévenet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Th%C3%A9venet "Bernard Thévenet") attacked on the lower slopes and Merckx was unable to counter.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013166-99)[Joop Zoetemelk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joop_Zoetemelk "Joop Zoetemelk") and [Luis Ocaña](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luis_Oca%C3%B1a "Luis Ocaña") went with Thévenet and wound up gaining 15 seconds on Merckx.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013166-99)

[![Image 23: A picture of a mountain.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/db/Col_du_Cucheron_-_Le_Planolet.JPG/250px-Col_du_Cucheron_-_Le_Planolet.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Col_du_Cucheron_-_Le_Planolet.JPG)

While descending the [Col du Cucheron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Col_du_Cucheron "Col du Cucheron") during the ninth stage of the [1971 Tour de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1971_Tour_de_France "1971 Tour de France"), Merckx suffered a puncture. Seeing this, his rivals attacked and wound up gaining 1' 30" on Merckx

On the descent of the [Col du Cucheron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Col_du_Cucheron "Col du Cucheron") during the race's ninth leg, Merckx's tire punctured, prompting Ocaña to attack with Zoetemelk, Thévenet, and [Gösta Pettersson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%B6sta_Pettersson "Gösta Pettersson").[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013166%E2%80%93167-100) The group of four finished a minute and a half ahead of Merckx, giving Zoetemelk the lead.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013167-101) The following day Merckx lost eight minutes to Ocaña after a poor showing due to stomach pains and indigestion.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013168%E2%80%93169-102) At the start of the eleventh stage, Merckx, three teammates, and a couple of others formed a breakaway.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013170-103) Merckx's group finished two minutes in front of the peloton that was led by Ocaña's Bic team.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013171-104) After winning the ensuing time trial, Merckx took back eleven more seconds on Ocaña.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013172-105) The race entered the [Pyrenees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenees "Pyrenees") with the first stage, into [Luchon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luchon "Luchon"), being plagued by heavy thunderstorms that severely handicapped vision.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013173-106) On the descent of the [Col de Menté](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Col_de_Ment%C3%A9 "Col de Menté"), Merckx crashed on a left bend.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013174-107) Ocaña, who was trailing, crashed into the same bend and Zoetemelk collided with him.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013174-107) Merckx fell again on the descent and took the race lead as Ocaña was forced to retire from the race due to injuries from the crash.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013175-108) Merckx declined to wear the yellow jersey the following day out of respect for Ocaña.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013175-108) He won two more stages and the general, points, and combination classifications when the race finished in Paris.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013175-108)[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013176-109)

Seven weeks following the Tour, Merckx entered the men's road race at the [UCI Road World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1971_UCI_Road_World_Championships "1971 UCI Road World Championships") that were held in [Mendrisio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mendrisio "Mendrisio"), Switzerland.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013179-110) The route for the day was rather hilly and consisted of several circuits.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013179-110) Merckx was a part of a five-man breakaway as the race reached five laps to go.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013179-110)

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/42/Eddy_Merckx_%28PANINI_%22Sprint_72%22_cover%29.jpg/250px-Eddy_Merckx_%28PANINI_%22Sprint_72%22_cover%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Eddy_Merckx_(PANINI_%22Sprint_72%22_cover).jpg)

Merckx followed by [Felice Gimondi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felice_Gimondi "Felice Gimondi") during the [1971 UCI Road World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1971_UCI_Road_World_Championships "1971 UCI Road World Championships") final

After attacking on the second to last stage, Merckx and Gimondi reached the finish, where Merckx won the race by four bike lengths.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013179-110) This earned him his second rainbow jersey.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013179-110) He closed out the 1971 calendar with his first victory in the [Giro di Lombardia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giro_di_Lombardia "Giro di Lombardia").[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013179-110) This victory meant that Merckx had won all of cycling's Monuments.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-sports-reference-2) Merckx made the winning move when he attacked on the descent of the Intelvi Pass.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013179-110) During the off-season, Merckx had his displaced pelvis tended to by a doctor.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013181-111)

#### 1972: Breaking the hour record alongside a Giro–Tour double

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Eddy_Merckx&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: 1972: Breaking the hour record alongside a Giro–Tour double")]

[![Image 25: A picture of a cyclist on a bike.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/72/Raymond_Poulidor%2C_Tour_de_France_1966_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Raymond_Poulidor%2C_Tour_de_France_1966_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Raymond_Poulidor,_Tour_de_France_1966_(cropped).jpg)

[Raymond Poulidor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raymond_Poulidor "Raymond Poulidor") (pictured at the [1966 Tour de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_Tour_de_France "1966 Tour de France")) won [1972 Paris–Nice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_Paris%E2%80%93Nice "1972 Paris–Nice") after taking the lead away from Merckx in the race's final stage, an individual time trial[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013182-112)

Merckx lost over two and a half minutes to Spanish climber [José Manuel Fuente](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Manuel_Fuente "José Manuel Fuente") after the Giro's fourth stage that contained a summit finish to Blockhaus.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013187-115) In the seventh stage, Fuente had attacked on the first climb of the day, the Valico di Monte Scuro.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013187-115) However, Fuente cracked near the top of the climb, allowing for Merckx and Pettersson to catch and pass him. Merckx gained over four minutes on Fuente and became the new race leader.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013187-115) He expanded his lead by two minutes through the stage 12a and 12b time trials, winning the former.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013188-116) Fuente got Merckx on his own as the two climbed together during the fourteenth stage.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013188-116) He and teammate [Francisco Galdós](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_Gald%C3%B3s "Francisco Galdós") attacked, leaving Merckx behind.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013188-116) Merckx eventually reconnected with the two on the final climb of the stage.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013188-116) He proceeded to attack and went on to win the stage by forty-seven seconds.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013188-116) He lost two minutes to Fuente due to stomach trouble during the seventeenth leg that finished atop the [Stelvio Pass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stelvio_Pass "Stelvio Pass"),[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013188-116) but went on to win one more stage en route to his third victory at the Giro d'Italia.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddy_Merckx#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFotheringham2013189-117)

A **bicycle**, also called a **pedal cycle**, **bike**, **push-bike** or **cycle**, is a [human-powered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human-powered_transport "Human-powered transport") or [motor-assisted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motorized_bicycle "Motorized bicycle"), [pedal-driven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_pedal "Bicycle pedal"), [single-track vehicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single-track_vehicle "Single-track vehicle"), with two [wheels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_wheel "Bicycle wheel") attached to a [frame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_frame "Bicycle frame"), one behind the other. A bicycle rider is called a [cyclist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling "Cycling") or bicyclist.

The bicycle was invented in Europe in the 19th century. By the early 21st century, there were more than 1 billion bicycles.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-Koeppel2007-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-Economist2011-2) Bicycles are the principal [means of transport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mode_of_transport "Mode of transport") in many regions. They are also popular for [recreation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recreation "Recreation"), and have been adapted for use as [children's toys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toy "Toy"). Bicycles are used for [commuting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commuting "Commuting"), [shopping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shopping "Shopping"), [fitness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physical_fitness "Physical fitness"), [military](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_bicycle "Military bicycle") and [police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police_bicycle "Police bicycle") applications, [courier services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_messenger "Bicycle messenger"), [bicycle racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycle_sport "Cycle sport"), and [artistic cycling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artistic_cycling "Artistic cycling").

The basic shape and configuration of a typical [upright or "safety" bicycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safety_bicycle "Safety bicycle"), has changed little since the first [chain-driven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chain_drive "Chain drive") model was developed around 1885.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHerlihy2004200%E2%80%9350-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHerlihy2004266%E2%80%9371-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHerlihy2004280-5) However, many details have been improved, especially since the advent of [modern materials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_materials "Modern materials") and [computer-aided design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer-aided_design "Computer-aided design"). These have allowed for a proliferation of specialized designs for many types of cycling. In the 21st century, [electric bicycles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_bicycle "Electric bicycle") have become popular.

The bicycle's invention has had an enormous effect on society, both in terms of [culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_culture "Bicycle culture") and of advancing modern [industrial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_industry "Bicycle industry") methods. Several components that played a key role in the development of the car were initially invented for use in the bicycle, including [ball bearings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ball_bearing "Ball bearing"), [pneumatic tires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tire "Tire"), [chain-driven sprockets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chain-driven_sprocket "Chain-driven sprocket"), and [tension-spoked wheels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wire_wheels "Wire wheels").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-6)

## Etymology

The first known appearance in English print of the word _bicycle_ was in _[The Daily News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Daily\_News\_(UK) "The Daily News (UK)")_ in 1868, to describe "Bysicles and trysicles" on the "[Champs Elysées](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Champs-%C3%89lys%C3%A9es "Champs-Élysées") and [Bois de Boulogne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bois_de_Boulogne "Bois de Boulogne")".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-OED-7) The word was first used in 1828 in French to describe a two-wheeled [chaise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaise "Chaise"), a horse-drawn carriage.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-OED-7) The design of the bicycle was an advance on the [velocipede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velocipede "Velocipede"), although the words were used with some degree of overlap for a time.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-OED-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-8)

Other words for bicycle include "bike",[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-9) "pushbike",[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-10) "pedal cycle",[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-11) or "cycle".[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-12) In [Unicode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unicode "Unicode"), the [code point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Code_point "Code point") for "bicycle" is U+1F6B2. The [entity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numeric_character_reference "Numeric character reference")`🚲` in [HTML](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTML "HTML") produces 🚲.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-13)

## History

This section is an excerpt from [History of the bicycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_bicycle "History of the bicycle").[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_the_bicycle&action=edit)]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5d/1886_Swift_Safety_Bicycle_Coventry_Transport_Museum.jpg/330px-1886_Swift_Safety_Bicycle_Coventry_Transport_Museum.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1886_Swift_Safety_Bicycle_Coventry_Transport_Museum.jpg)

1886 Swift Safety Bicycle

The "[dandy horse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dandy_horse "Dandy horse")",[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-14) also called _Draisienne_ or _Laufmaschine_ ("running machine"), was the first human means of transport to use only two wheels in [tandem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tandem "Tandem") and was invented by the German [Baron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freiherr "Freiherr")[Karl von Drais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Drais "Karl Drais"). It is regarded as the first bicycle and von Drais is seen as the "father of the bicycle",[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-History_of_the_bicycle_:0-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-History_of_the_bicycle_:1-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-History_of_the_bicycle_:2-17) but it did not have pedals.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-20) Von Drais introduced it to the public in [Mannheim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mannheim "Mannheim") in 1817 and in Paris in 1818.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-History_of_the_bicycle_csts-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHerlihy200426-22) The rider sat astride a wooden frame supported by two in-line wheels and pushed the vehicle along with their feet while steering the front wheel.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-History_of_the_bicycle_csts-21)

The [first mechanically propelled, two-wheeled vehicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treadle_bicycle "Treadle bicycle") may have been built by [Kirkpatrick MacMillan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirkpatrick_MacMillan "Kirkpatrick MacMillan"), a Scottish blacksmith, in 1839, although this claim is often disputed.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHerlihy200466%E2%80%9367-23) He is also associated with the first recorded instance of a cycling traffic offense, when a Glasgow newspaper in 1842 reported an accident in which an anonymous "gentleman from Dumfries-shire... bestride a velocipede... of ingenious design" knocked over a little girl in Glasgow and was fined five [shillings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shilling "Shilling") (equivalent to £24 in 2025).[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-24)

In the early 1860s, the Frenchmen [Pierre Michaux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Michaux "Pierre Michaux") and [Pierre Lallement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Lallement "Pierre Lallement") took bicycle design in a new direction by adding a mechanical [crank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crank_(mechanism) "Crank (mechanism)") drive with pedals on an enlarged front wheel (the [velocipede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velocipede "Velocipede")). This was the first in mass production. Another French inventor named Douglas Grasso had a failed prototype of Pierre Lallement's bicycle several years earlier. Several inventions followed using rear-wheel drive, the best known being the rod-driven velocipede by Scotsman [Thomas McCall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_McCall_(inventor) "Thomas McCall (inventor)") in 1869. In the same year, bicycle wheels with wire spokes were patented by [Eugène Meyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eug%C3%A8ne_Meyer_(inventor) "Eugène Meyer (inventor)") of Paris.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-25) The French _vélocipède_, made of iron and wood, developed into the "[penny-farthing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny-farthing "Penny-farthing")" (historically known as an "ordinary bicycle", a [retronym](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retronym "Retronym"), since there was then no other kind).[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-FOOTNOTENorcliffe200150-26) It featured a tubular steel frame on which were mounted wire-spoked wheels with solid rubber tires. These bicycles were difficult to mount, dismount and brake due to their high seat over the large front wheel. In 1868, Rowley Turner, a sales agent of the Coventry Sewing Machine Company (which soon became the [Coventry Machinists Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillman#History "Hillman")), brought a Michaux cycle to [Coventry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coventry "Coventry"), England. His uncle, Josiah Turner, and business partner [James Starley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Starley "James Starley"), used this as a basis for the 'Coventry Model' in what became Britain's first cycle factory.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-27)

The _dwarf ordinary_ addressed some of these faults by reducing the front wheel [diameter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diameter "Diameter") and setting the [seat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_seat "Bicycle seat") further back. This, in turn, required gearing—effected in a variety of ways—to efficiently use pedal power. Having to both pedal and steer via the front wheel remained a problem. Englishman [J.K. Starley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kemp_Starley "John Kemp Starley") (nephew of James Starley), J.H. Lawson, and Shergold solved this problem by introducing the [chain drive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chain_drive "Chain drive") (originated by the unsuccessful "bicyclette" of Englishman Henry Lawson),[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-FOOTNOTENorcliffe200147-28) connecting the frame-mounted cranks to the rear wheel. These models were known as [safety bicycles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safety_bicycle "Safety bicycle"), dwarf safeties, or upright bicycles for their lower seat height. Although, without pneumatic tires, the ride of the smaller-wheeled bicycle would be much rougher than that of the larger-wheeled variety. Starley's 1885 [Rover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rover_Company "Rover Company"), manufactured in Coventry[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-29) is usually described as the first recognizably modern bicycle.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-30) Soon, the _seat tube_ was added, which created the modern bike's double-triangle _diamond frame_.

Further innovations increased comfort and ushered in a second [bicycle craze](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_craze "Bicycle craze"), the 1890s _Golden Age of Bicycles_. In 1888, Scotsman [John Boyd Dunlop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Boyd_Dunlop "John Boyd Dunlop") introduced the first practical pneumatic tire, which soon became universal. [Willie Hume](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Hume "Willie Hume") demonstrated the supremacy of Dunlop's tyres in 1889, winning the tyre's first-ever races in Ireland and then England.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-History_of_the_bicycle_Gold_Hume-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-History_of_the_bicycle_Dunlop_time-32) Soon after, the rear [freewheel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freewheel "Freewheel") was developed, enabling the rider to coast. This refinement led to the 1890s invention[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-33) of [coaster brakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coaster_brake "Coaster brake"). [Derailleur gears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derailleur_gears "Derailleur gears") and hand-operated [Bowden cable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowden_cable "Bowden cable")-pull brakes were also developed during these years, but were only slowly adopted by casual riders.

The [Svea Velocipede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Svea_Velocipede "Svea Velocipede") with vertical pedal arrangement and [locking hubs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locking_hubs "Locking hubs") was introduced in 1892 by the Swedish engineers [Fredrik Ljungström](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredrik_Ljungstr%C3%B6m "Fredrik Ljungström") and [Birger Ljungström](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birger_Ljungstr%C3%B6m "Birger Ljungström").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-34)

In the 1870s, many [cycling clubs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_club "Cycling club") flourished. They were popular in a time when there were no cars on the market and the principal mode of transportation was [horse-drawn vehicles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horse-drawn_vehicle "Horse-drawn vehicle"). Among the earliest clubs was [The Bicycle Touring Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_UK "Cycling UK"), which has operated since 1878. By the turn of the century, cycling clubs flourished on both sides of the Atlantic, and touring and racing became widely popular. The [Raleigh Bicycle Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raleigh_Bicycle_Company "Raleigh Bicycle Company") was founded in [Nottingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nottingham "Nottingham"), England in 1888. It became the biggest bicycle manufacturer in the world, making over two million bikes per year.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-35)

Bicycles and [horse buggies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buggy_(carriage) "Buggy (carriage)") were the two mainstays of private transportation just prior to the automobile, and the grading of smooth roads in the late 19th century was stimulated by the widespread advertising, production, and use of these devices.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHerlihy2004280-5) More than 1 billion bicycles had been manufactured worldwide by the early 21st century.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-History_of_the_bicycle_Koeppel2007-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-History_of_the_bicycle_Economist2011-37) Bicycles are the most common vehicle of any kind in the world, and the most numerous model of any kind of vehicle, whether human-powered or [motor vehicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motor_vehicle "Motor vehicle"), is the Chinese [Flying Pigeon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flying_Pigeon "Flying Pigeon"), with numbers exceeding 500 million.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-History_of_the_bicycle_Koeppel2007-36)
