## Uses

Main article: [Cycling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling "Cycling")

Bicycles are used for transportation, [bicycle commuting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_commuting "Bicycle commuting"), and [utility cycling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utility_cycling "Utility cycling").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-38)[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_] The [energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy "Energy") taken to cycle to a particular distance takes less than the energy to [walk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walking "Walking") as far by four-fifths or 80 percent.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilson197382-39) They are also used professionally by [mail carriers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_mail "Bicycle mail"), [paramedics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramedic "Paramedic"), [police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police_bicycle "Police bicycle"), [messengers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_messenger "Bicycle messenger"), and [for deliveries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cargo_bike "Cargo bike"). Military uses of bicycles included [communications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_communications "Military communications"), [reconnaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconnaissance "Reconnaissance"), troop movement, supply of provisions, and patrol, such as in [bicycle infantries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_infantry "Bicycle infantry").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-40)

They are also used for fun, including [bicycle touring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_touring "Bicycle touring"), [mountain biking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain_biking "Mountain biking"), [physical fitness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physical_fitness "Physical fitness"), and [play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Play_(activity) "Play (activity)"). [Bicycle sports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycle_sport "Cycle sport") include [racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_bicycle_racing "Road bicycle racing"), [BMX racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BMX_racing "BMX racing"), [track racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Track_cycling "Track cycling"), [criterium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criterium "Criterium"), [roller racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_rollers "Bicycle rollers"), [sportives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclosportive "Cyclosportive") and [time trials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_trial "Time trial"). They are also used for entertainment and pleasure in other ways, such as in organised mass rides, [artistic cycling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artistic_cycling "Artistic cycling") and [freestyle BMX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freestyle_BMX "Freestyle BMX").

### Dynamics

Main article: [Bicycle and motorcycle dynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_and_motorcycle_dynamics "Bicycle and motorcycle dynamics")

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1b/Jersey_Town_Criterium_2011_81.jpg/250px-Jersey_Town_Criterium_2011_81.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jersey_Town_Criterium_2011_81.jpg)

A cyclist leaning in a turn

A bicycle stays upright while moving forward by being steered so as to keep its [center of mass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_of_mass "Center of mass") over the wheels, that is in line with the resultant force of gravity and centrifugal force.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-NS2581-45) This steering is usually provided by the rider, but under certain conditions, may be provided by the bicycle itself.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-MPRS-46)

The combined center of mass of a bicycle and its rider must lean into a turn. This lean is induced by a method known as [countersteering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Countersteering "Countersteering"), which can be performed by the rider turning the handlebars directly with the hands[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-Wilson-47) or indirectly by leaning the bicycle.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-fajans-48)

Short-wheelbase or tall bicycles, when braking, can generate enough stopping force at the front wheel to flip longitudinally.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-49) The act of purposefully using this force to lift the rear wheel and balance on the front without tipping over is a trick known as a [stoppie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoppie "Stoppie"), endo, or front wheelie.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-50)

### Performance

Main article: [Bicycle performance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_performance "Bicycle performance")

The bicycle is extraordinarily efficient in both biological and mechanical terms. The bicycle is the most efficient human-powered means of transportation in terms of energy a person must expend to travel a given distance, when travelling slowly or equipped with an aerodynamic fairing. From a mechanical viewpoint, up to 99% of the energy delivered by the rider into the pedals is transmitted to the wheels, although the use of gearing mechanisms may reduce this by 10–15% and there is also a small amount of tire slip.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-whitt-52)

A human traveling on a bicycle at low to medium speeds of about 16–24 km/h (10–15 mph) uses only the power required to walk. Air drag, which is proportional to the square of speed, requires dramatically higher power outputs as speeds increase. If the rider is sitting upright, the rider's body creates about 75% of the total drag of the bicycle/rider combination. Drag can be reduced by seating the rider in a more [aerodynamically](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerodynamic "Aerodynamic") streamlined position. Drag can also be reduced by covering the bicycle with an aerodynamic [fairing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_fairing "Bicycle fairing"). The fastest recorded unpaced speed on a flat surface with a standing start was the hour record in 2016: over 92 km/h (57 mph) with a highly streamlined bicycle.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-53)

### Frame

Main article: [Bicycle frame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_frame "Bicycle frame")

Most modern bicycles have a frame with upright seating that looks much like the first chain-driven bike.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHerlihy2004200%E2%80%9350-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHerlihy2004266%E2%80%9371-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHerlihy2004280-5) These upright bicycles frequently have a _diamond frame_, a [truss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truss "Truss") consisting of two triangles: the front triangle and the rear triangle. The front triangle consists of the top tube and down tube (connected by the head tube), and seat tube. The head tube contains the [headset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Headset_(bicycle_part) "Headset (bicycle part)"), the set of bearings that allows the [fork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_fork "Bicycle fork") to turn smoothly for steering and balance. The rear triangle consists of the seat tube, with the [bottom bracket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bottom_bracket "Bottom bracket") at the bottom, and paired _chain stays_ and _seat stays_, connecting at the rear [dropouts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fork_end "Fork end"), where the axle for the rear wheel is held.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-55) The frame's shape allows the rider's weight to be distributed in a way that does not misshapen or compress the entire frame as it turns.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilson197385-56)

Historically, women's bicycle frames had a top tube that connected in the middle of the seat tube instead of the top, resulting in a lower [standover height](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frame_geometry "Frame geometry") at the expense of compromised structural integrity, since this places a strong bending load in the seat tube, and bicycle frame members are typically weak in bending. This design, referred to as a _[step-through frame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Step-through\_frame "Step-through frame")_ or as an _open frame_, allows the rider to mount and dismount in a dignified way while wearing a skirt or dress. While some women's bicycles continue to use this frame style, there is also a variation, the _[mixte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixte "Mixte")_, which splits the top tube laterally into two thinner top tubes that bypass the seat tube on each side and connect to the rear fork ends.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-57)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-59)

Another style is the [recumbent bicycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recumbent_bicycle "Recumbent bicycle"). These are inherently more aerodynamic than upright versions, as the rider may lean back onto a support and operate pedals that are on about the same level as the seat. The world's fastest bicycle is a recumbent bicycle but this type was banned from competition in 1934 by the [Union Cycliste Internationale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Cycliste_Internationale "Union Cycliste Internationale").[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-60)

Historically, materials used in bicycles have followed a similar pattern as in aircraft, the goal being high strength and low weight. Since the late 1930s, alloy steels have been used for frame and fork tubes in higher quality machines. By the 1980s, [aluminum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminum "Aluminum")[welding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welding "Welding") techniques had improved to the point that aluminum tube could safely be used instead of [steel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steel "Steel"). Since then aluminum alloy frames and other components have become popular due to their light weight, and most mid-range bikes are now aluminum alloy. More expensive bikes sometimes use [titanium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titanium "Titanium") or more often [carbon fibre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_fibre "Carbon fibre") laid-up in resin due to its significantly lighter weight and profiling ability, allowing designers to make a bike both stiff and compliant by arranging the angles of the laid-up fibres optimally. Virtually all professional racing bicycles now use carbon fibre frames, as they have the best strength to weight ratio. A typical modern carbon fiber frame can weigh less than 2 pounds (1 kg).[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-61)

Wood and [bamboo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bamboo "Bamboo"), a natural [composite material](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Composite_material "Composite material") with high strength-to-weight ratio and [stiffness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stiffness "Stiffness"),[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-Lakkad-62) have been used for bicycles since 1894.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-lukenbill-63) Modern versions use bamboo for the primary frame with glued metal connections and parts.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-lukenbill-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-65)

### Drivetrain and gearing

Main article: [Bicycle drivetrain systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_drivetrain_systems "Bicycle drivetrain systems")

The _drivetrain_ begins with pedals which rotate the [cranks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crank_set "Crank set"), which are held in axis by the bottom bracket. Most bicycles use a chain to transmit power to the rear wheel. A very small number of bicycles use a shaft drive to transmit power. Hydraulic bicycle transmissions have been built, but they can be inefficient and complex.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-:0-66)

Since cyclists' legs are most efficient over a narrow range of pedaling speeds, or [cadence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cadence_(cycling) "Cadence (cycling)"), a variable [gear ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gear_ratio "Gear ratio") helps a cyclist to maintain an optimum pedalling speed while covering varied terrain. Some, mainly utility, bicycles use [hub gears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hub_gear "Hub gear") with between 3 and 14 ratios, but most use the generally more efficient [derailleur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derailleur "Derailleur") system, by which the chain is moved between different cogs called chainrings and sprockets to select a ratio. A derailleur system normally has two derailleurs, or mechs, one at the front to select the [chainring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chainring "Chainring") and another at the back to select the sprocket. Most bikes have two or three chainrings, and from 5 to 12 sprockets on the back, with the number of theoretical gears calculated by multiplying front by back. In reality, many gears overlap or require the chain to run diagonally, so the number of usable gears is fewer.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-:0-66)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-67)

An alternative to chain drive is to use a toothed belt. These work much the same as a chain, they are popular with commuters as they require little maintenance. They are slightly less efficient than chains and cannot be shifted across a cassette of sprockets, and are used either as single speed or with a hub gear.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-:1-68)

[Different gears and ranges of gears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_gearing "Bicycle gearing") are appropriate for different people and styles of cycling. Multi-speed bicycles allow gear selection to suit the circumstances: a cyclist could use a high gear when cycling downhill, a medium gear when cycling on a flat road, and a low gear when cycling uphill. In a lower gear, every turn of the pedals leads to fewer rotations of the rear wheel. This allows the energy required to move the same distance to be distributed over more pedal turns, reducing fatigue when riding uphill, with a heavy load, or against strong winds. A higher gear allows a cyclist to make fewer pedal turns to maintain a given speed, but with more effort per turn of the pedals.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-69)

With a _chain drive_ transmission, a _chainring_ attached to a crank drives the chain, which in turn rotates the rear wheel via the rear sprocket(s) ([cassette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassette_(bicycle_part) "Cassette (bicycle part)") or [freewheel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cogset#Freewheels "Cogset")). There are four gearing options: two-speed hub gear integrated with chain ring, up to 3 chain rings, up to 12 sprockets and hub gear built into rear wheel (3-speed to 14-speed). The most common options are either a rear hub or multiple chain rings combined with multiple sprockets (other combinations of options are possible but less common).

### Steering

[![Image 35](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/Anatomic_bicycle_grips_made_of_leather.jpg/250px-Anatomic_bicycle_grips_made_of_leather.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Anatomic_bicycle_grips_made_of_leather.jpg)

Bicycle grips made of leather. Anatomic shape distributes weight over [palm area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hand "Hand") to prevent cyclist's palsy ([ulnar syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulnar_tunnel_syndrome "Ulnar tunnel syndrome")).[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-70)

The [handlebars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_handlebar "Bicycle handlebar") connect to the [stem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stem_(bike) "Stem (bike)") that connects to the fork housing the front wheel. The whole assembly rotates about the steering axis, held by the [headset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Headset_(bicycle_part) "Headset (bicycle part)") bearings.

Three styles of handlebar are common. _Upright handlebars_, the norm in Europe and elsewhere until the 1970s, curve gently back towards the rider, offering a natural grip and comfortable upright position. _Drop handlebars_ "drop" as they curve forward and down, allowing the cyclist to use either a more aerodynamic "crouched" position or a more upright position. Mountain bikes generally feature a 'straight handlebar' or 'riser bar' with varying degrees of sweep backward and centimeters rise upwards, as well as wider widths which can provide better handling due to increased leverage against the wheel.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-71)

### Seating

[![Image 36](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/58/San_marco_selle1.jpg/250px-San_marco_selle1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:San_marco_selle1.jpg)

A Selle San Marco saddle designed for women

[Saddles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_saddle "Bicycle saddle") also vary with rider preference, from the cushioned ones favored by short-distance riders to narrower saddles which allow more room for leg swings. Comfort depends on riding position.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-72) With comfort bikes and hybrids, cyclists sit high over the seat, their weight directed down onto the saddle, such that a wider and more cushioned saddle is preferable. For racing bikes where the rider is bent over, weight is more evenly distributed between the handlebars and saddle, the hips are flexed, and a narrower and harder saddle is more efficient. Differing saddle designs exist for male and female cyclists, accommodating the genders' differing anatomies and sit bone width measurements,[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-73) although bikes are typically sold with saddles most appropriate for men. Suspension seat posts and seat springs provide comfort by absorbing shock but can add to the overall weight of the bicycle.

A recumbent bicycle has a reclined [chair-like seat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_seat "Bicycle seat") that some riders find more comfortable than a saddle, especially riders who suffer from certain types of seat, back, neck, shoulder, or wrist pain. Recumbent bicycles may have either under-seat or over-seat [steering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recumbent_bicycle#Steering "Recumbent bicycle").

### Brakes

Main article: [Bicycle brake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_brake "Bicycle brake")

[![Image 37](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4b/Brake.agr-edit.jpg/250px-Brake.agr-edit.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Brake.agr-edit.jpg)

Linear-pull brake, also known by the [Shimano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shimano "Shimano") trademark: V-Brake, on rear wheel of a [mountain bike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain_bike "Mountain bike")

Bicycle brakes may be rim brakes, in which friction pads are compressed against the wheel rims; hub brakes, where the mechanism is contained within the wheel hub; or disc brakes, where pads act on a rotor attached to the hub. Most road bicycles use rim brakes, but some use disc brakes.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-74)[Disc brakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disc_brakes "Disc brakes") are more common for mountain bikes, tandems and recumbent bicycles than on other types of bicycles, due to their increased power, coupled with an increased weight and complexity.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-75)

[![Image 38](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/21/BrakeDiskVR.JPG/250px-BrakeDiskVR.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:BrakeDiskVR.JPG)

A front disc brake, mounted to the [fork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_fork "Bicycle fork") and hub

With hand-operated brakes, force is applied to brake levers mounted on the handlebars and transmitted via Bowden cables or [hydraulic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydraulic "Hydraulic") lines to the friction pads, which apply pressure to the braking surface, causing friction which slows the bicycle down. A rear hub brake may be either hand-operated or pedal-actuated, as in the back pedal _coaster brakes_ which were popular in North America until the 1960s.

[Track bicycles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Track_bicycle "Track bicycle") do not have brakes, because all riders ride in the same direction around a track which does not necessitate sharp deceleration. Track riders are still able to slow down because all track bicycles are fixed-gear, meaning that there is no freewheel. Without a freewheel, coasting is impossible, so when the rear wheel is moving, the cranks are moving. To slow down, the rider applies resistance to the pedals, acting as a braking system which can be as effective as a conventional rear wheel brake, but not as effective as a front wheel brake.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-76)

### Suspension

Main article: [Bicycle suspension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_suspension "Bicycle suspension")

Bicycle suspension refers to the system or systems used to _suspend_ the rider and all or part of the bicycle. This serves two purposes: to keep the wheels in continuous contact with the ground, improving control, and to isolate the rider and luggage from jarring due to rough surfaces, improving comfort.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-:2-77)

Bicycle suspensions are used primarily on mountain bicycles, but are also common on hybrid bicycles, as they can help deal with problematic vibration from poor surfaces. Suspension is especially important on recumbent bicycles, since while an upright bicycle rider can stand on the pedals to achieve some of the benefits of suspension, a recumbent rider cannot.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-:2-77)

Basic mountain bicycles and hybrids usually have front suspension only, whilst more sophisticated ones also have rear suspension. Road bicycles tend to have no suspension.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-:2-77)

### Wheels and tires

Main articles: [Bicycle wheel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_wheel "Bicycle wheel") and [Bicycle tire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_tire "Bicycle tire")

[![Image 39](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6d/Cykeld%C3%A4ck_-_Bike_tyres_-_2025.jpg/250px-Cykeld%C3%A4ck_-_Bike_tyres_-_2025.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cykeld%C3%A4ck_-_Bike_tyres_-_2025.jpg)

Two tires of the same make and tread pattern, the lower one completely unused, the upper one has rolled over 1,500 km (900 mi) on varying surfaces.

The wheel axle fits into fork ends in the frame and fork. A pair of wheels may be called a wheelset, especially in the context of ready-built "off the shelf", performance-oriented wheels. Tires vary enormously depending on their intended purpose. [Road bicycles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_bicycles "Road bicycles") typically use tires from 25 mm (1 in) to 35 mm (1.4 in) wide,[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-78) sometimes completely smooth, or [slick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slick_tire "Slick tire"), and inflated to high pressure to roll fast on smooth surfaces. Off-road tires are usually wider, from 30 mm (1.2 in) to 100 mm (4 in),[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-79) and have treads for gripping in muddy conditions or metal studs for ice.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-80)

### Accessories

[![Image 40](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a3/Loaded_touring_bicycle.JPG/250px-Loaded_touring_bicycle.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Loaded_touring_bicycle.JPG)

Touring bicycle equipped with front and rear [racks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luggage_carrier "Luggage carrier"), fenders (called mud-guards), water bottles in [cages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bottle_cage "Bottle cage"), four [panniers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pannier "Pannier") and a handlebar bag

Some components, which are often optional accessories on sports bicycles, are standard features on utility bicycles to enhance their usefulness, comfort, safety and visibility. [Fenders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fender_(vehicle) "Fender (vehicle)") with spoilers (mudflaps) protect the cyclist and moving parts from spray when riding through wet areas. In some countries (e.g. Germany, UK), fenders are called mudguards. The [chainguards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chainguard "Chainguard") protect clothes from oil on the chain while preventing clothing from being caught between the chain and [crankset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crankset "Crankset") teeth. [Kick stands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kick_stand "Kick stand") keep bicycles upright when parked, and [bike locks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike_lock "Bike lock") deter theft. Front-mounted [baskets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_basket "Bicycle basket"), front or rear [luggage carriers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luggage_carrier "Luggage carrier") or racks, and [panniers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pannier "Pannier") mounted above either or both wheels can be used to carry equipment or cargo. Parents sometimes add rear-mounted [child seats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baby_transport "Baby transport"), an auxiliary saddle fitted to the crossbar, or both to transport children. Bicycles can also be fitted with a hitch to tow a [trailer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_trailer "Bicycle trailer") for carrying cargo, a child, or both.

[Toe-clips](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clipless#Clipless_pedals "Clipless"), toestraps and [clipless pedals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clipless_pedals "Clipless pedals") help keep the foot locked in the proper pedal position and enable cyclists to pull and push the pedals. Technical accessories include [cyclocomputers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclocomputer "Cyclocomputer") for measuring speed, distance, heart rate, GPS data etc. Other accessories include [lights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_lighting "Bicycle lighting"), reflectors, mirrors, racks, trailers, bags, water bottles and [cages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bottle_cage "Bottle cage"), and [bells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_bell "Bicycle bell").[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-bicycleuniverse-81) Bicycle lights, reflectors, and helmets are required by law in some geographic regions. It is more common to see bicycles with bottle generators, dynamos, lights, fenders, racks and bells in Europe. Bicyclists also have specialized form fitting and high visibility clothing.

Children's bicycles may be outfitted with cosmetic enhancements such as [bike horns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_horn "Bicycle horn"), streamers, and [spoke beads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spoke_beads "Spoke beads").[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-82)[Training wheels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Training_wheels "Training wheels") are sometimes used when learning to ride, but a dedicated [balance bike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balance_bike "Balance bike") teaches independent riding more effectively.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-83)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-84)

[Bicycle helmets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_helmet "Bicycle helmet") can reduce injury in the event of a collision or accident, and a suitable helmet is legally required of riders in many jurisdictions.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-85)[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-86) Helmets may be classified as an accessory[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-bicycleuniverse-81) or as an item of clothing.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-87)

[Bike trainers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_trainer "Bicycle trainer") are used to enable cyclists to cycle while the bike remains stationary. They are frequently used to warm up before races or indoors when riding conditions are unfavorable.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-88)

### Standards

A number of formal and industry standards exist for bicycle components to help make spare parts exchangeable and to maintain a minimum product safety. The [International Organization for Standardization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Organization_for_Standardization "International Organization for Standardization") (ISO) has a special technical committee for cycles, TC149, that has the scope of "Standardization in the field of cycles, their components and accessories with particular reference to terminology, testing methods and requirements for performance and safety, and interchangeability".[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-89)

The [European Committee for Standardization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Committee_for_Standardization "European Committee for Standardization") (CEN) also has a specific Technical Committee, TC333, that defines European standards for cycles. Their mandate states that CEN cycle standards shall harmonize with [ISO standards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ISO_standards "List of ISO standards"). Some CEN cycle standards were developed before ISO published their standards, leading to strong European influences in this area. European cycle standards tend to describe minimum safety requirements, while ISO standards have historically harmonized parts geometry.[[note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-90)[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-91)

The [bicycle industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_industry "Bicycle industry") or cycling industry can broadly be defined as the [industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industry_(economics) "Industry (economics)") concerned with [bicycles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycles "Bicycles") and [cycling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling "Cycling"). It includes at least [bicycle manufacturers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_bicycle_manufacturers "List of bicycle manufacturers"), part or component manufacturers, and accessory manufacturers. It can also include [distributors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_(business) "Distribution (business)"), [retailers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retailing "Retailing"), bicycle organizations, bicycle event promoters, and bicycle related service providers.

The global bicycle industry generated sales of $66 billion in 2024.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-92)

### Manufacturing and sales

These paragraphs are an excerpt from [List of bicycle brands and manufacturing companies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_bicycle_brands_and_manufacturing_companies "List of bicycle brands and manufacturing companies").[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_bicycle_brands_and_manufacturing_companies&action=edit)]

Over 100 million bicycles are made each year, the top three manufacturing countries being China, India and Taiwan.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-93) In 2025, the global market size was an estimated $116 billion.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-94)

Many bicycle brands do not manufacture their own product, but rather import and re-brand bikes manufactured by others, sometimes designing the bike, specifying the equipment, and providing quality control. There are also brands that have, at different times, been manufacturers as well as [re-branders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Badge_engineering "Badge engineering"): a company with manufacturing capability may market models made by other (overseas) factories, while simultaneously manufacturing bicycles in-house, for example, high-end models.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-95)

## Maintenance and repair

[![Image 42](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b4/Frankfurt%2C_Germany_-_Woolworth_bicycle_accessories.jpg/250px-Frankfurt%2C_Germany_-_Woolworth_bicycle_accessories.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Frankfurt,_Germany_-_Woolworth_bicycle_accessories.jpg)

Bicycle maintenance section in a [Woolworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woolworth_(Europe) "Woolworth (Europe)") in [Frankfurt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frankfurt "Frankfurt") offering various parts and tools like pumps, lights, bells, handlebar grips, saddles, brakes and inner tubes

A bicycle can be kept in good condition for decades.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-:4-54) Like all products with mechanical moving parts, bicycles require regular maintenance and replacement of worn parts. A bicycle is relatively simple compared with a car, so some cyclists choose to do at least part of the maintenance themselves. Some components are easy to manage using relatively simple tools, while other components may require specialist manufacturer-dependent tools.

Many bicycle components are available at several different price/quality points; manufacturers generally try to keep all components on any particular bike at about the same quality level, though at the very cheap end of the market there may be some skimping on less obvious components (e.g. bottom bracket).

*   There are several hundred assisted-service community bicycle organizations worldwide.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-96) At a community bicycle organization, [laypeople](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/layperson#Noun "wikt:layperson") bring in bicycles needing repair or maintenance; volunteers teach them how to do the required steps.
*   Full services are available from [bicycle mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_mechanic "Bicycle mechanic") at [local bike shops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_bike_shop "Local bike shop").
*   In areas where it is available, some cyclists purchase roadside assistance from companies such as the [Better World Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Better_World_Club "Better World Club") or the [American Automobile Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Automobile_Association "American Automobile Association").

### Maintenance

Keeping the tires correctly inflated can make a noticeable difference as to how the bike feels to ride. Bicycle tires usually have a marking on the sidewall indicating the pressure appropriate for that tire, from 100 to 1,400 kPa (15 to 200 psi).[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-97) Over the longer term, tires wear out, after 1,500 to 5,000 kilometres (900 to 3,000 miles); with punctures often the most visible sign of a worn tire.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-98)

Many community cycling organisations will check brakes and other basic parts for free, or bike shops at low cost.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-:3-99) Disc brakes can be cleaned[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-100) but may need professional maintenance, but rim brakes are easier to adjust.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-:3-99)

Chains can be washed with soapy water then lightly lubricated, but may need replacing after a couple of years.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-:3-99) Other parts, such as derailleur pivot points, can also be lubricated, but lightly as dirt may stick with too much oil.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-101)

### Repair

Very few bicycle components can actually be repaired; replacement of the failing component is normal practice.

The most common roadside problem is a puncture of the tire's [inner tube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_tube "Inner tube"). A patch kit may be employed to fix the puncture or the tube can be replaced, though the latter solution comes at a greater cost and waste of material.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-Guardian-102) Some brands of tires are much more [puncture-resistant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puncture_resistance "Puncture resistance") than others, often incorporating one or more layers of [Kevlar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevlar "Kevlar"); the downside of such tires is that they may be heavier and more difficult to fit and remove.

### Tools

Main article: [Bicycle tools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_tools "Bicycle tools")

[![Image 43](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/Puncture-repaire-kit.jpg/250px-Puncture-repaire-kit.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Puncture-repaire-kit.jpg)

Puncture repair kit with tire levers, [sandpaper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandpaper "Sandpaper") to clean off an area of the [inner tube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_tube "Inner tube") around the puncture, a tube of rubber solution ([vulcanizing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulcanization "Vulcanization") fluid), round and oval patches, a metal grater and piece of chalk to make chalk powder (to dust over excess rubber solution). Kits often also include a wax crayon to mark the puncture location.

There are specialized bicycle tools for use both in the shop and at the roadside. Many cyclists carry tool kits. These may include a tire patch kit (which, in turn, may contain any combination of a [hand pump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_pump "Bicycle pump") or [CO 2 pump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_pump#CO2_Inflators "Bicycle pump"), [tire levers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tire_lever "Tire lever"), spare [tubes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_tube "Inner tube"), self-adhesive patches, or tube-patching material, an adhesive, a piece of sandpaper or a metal grater (for roughening the tube surface to be patched) and sometimes even a block of [French chalk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_chalk "French chalk")), [wrenches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wrench "Wrench"), [hex keys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hex_key "Hex key"), screwdrivers, and a [chain tool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chain_tool "Chain tool"). Special, thin wrenches are often required for maintaining various screw-fastened parts, specifically, the frequently lubricated ball-bearing "cones".[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-103)[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-104) There are also cycling-specific [multi-tools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-tool "Multi-tool") that combine many of these implements into a single compact device. More specialized bicycle components may require more complex tools, including proprietary tools specific for a given manufacturer.

## Social and historical aspects

The bicycle has had a considerable effect on human society, in both the cultural and industrial realms.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-105)[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-106)

Around the turn of the 20th century, bicycles reduced crowding in inner-city tenements by allowing workers to commute from more spacious dwellings in the suburbs. They also reduced dependence on horses. Bicycles allowed people to travel for leisure into the country, since bicycles were three times as energy efficient as walking and three to four times as fast.

Classic bell of a bicycle

A **bicycle**, also called a **pedal cycle**, **bike**, **push-bike** or **cycle**, is a [human-powered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human-powered_transport "Human-powered transport") or [motor-assisted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motorized_bicycle "Motorized bicycle"), [pedal-driven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_pedal "Bicycle pedal"), [single-track vehicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single-track_vehicle "Single-track vehicle"), with two [wheels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_wheel "Bicycle wheel") attached to a [frame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_frame "Bicycle frame"), one behind the other. A bicycle rider is called a [cyclist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling "Cycling") or bicyclist.

The bicycle was invented in Europe in the 19th century. By the early 21st century, there were more than 1 billion bicycles.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-Koeppel2007-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-Economist2011-2) Bicycles are the principal [means of transport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mode_of_transport "Mode of transport") in many regions. They are also popular for [recreation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recreation "Recreation"), and have been adapted for use as [children's toys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toy "Toy"). Bicycles are used for [commuting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commuting "Commuting"), [shopping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shopping "Shopping"), [fitness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physical_fitness "Physical fitness"), [military](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_bicycle "Military bicycle") and [police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police_bicycle "Police bicycle") applications, [courier services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_messenger "Bicycle messenger"), [bicycle racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycle_sport "Cycle sport"), and [artistic cycling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artistic_cycling "Artistic cycling").

The basic shape and configuration of a typical [upright or "safety" bicycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safety_bicycle "Safety bicycle"), has changed little since the first [chain-driven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chain_drive "Chain drive") model was developed around 1885.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHerlihy2004200%E2%80%9350-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHerlihy2004266%E2%80%9371-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHerlihy2004280-5) However, many details have been improved, especially since the advent of [modern materials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_materials "Modern materials") and [computer-aided design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer-aided_design "Computer-aided design"). These have allowed for a proliferation of specialized designs for many types of cycling. In the 21st century, [electric bicycles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_bicycle "Electric bicycle") have become popular.

The bicycle's invention has had an enormous effect on society, both in terms of [culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_culture "Bicycle culture") and of advancing modern [industrial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_industry "Bicycle industry") methods. Several components that played a key role in the development of the car were initially invented for use in the bicycle, including [ball bearings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ball_bearing "Ball bearing"), [pneumatic tires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tire "Tire"), [chain-driven sprockets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chain-driven_sprocket "Chain-driven sprocket"), and [tension-spoked wheels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wire_wheels "Wire wheels").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-6)

## Etymology

The first known appearance in English print of the word _bicycle_ was in _[The Daily News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Daily\_News\_(UK) "The Daily News (UK)")_ in 1868, to describe "Bysicles and trysicles" on the "[Champs Elysées](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Champs-%C3%89lys%C3%A9es "Champs-Élysées") and [Bois de Boulogne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bois_de_Boulogne "Bois de Boulogne")".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-OED-7) The word was first used in 1828 in French to describe a two-wheeled [chaise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaise "Chaise"), a horse-drawn carriage.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-OED-7) The design of the bicycle was an advance on the [velocipede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velocipede "Velocipede"), although the words were used with some degree of overlap for a time.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-OED-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-8)

Other words for bicycle include "bike",[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-9) "pushbike",[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-10) "pedal cycle",[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-11) or "cycle".[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-12) In [Unicode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unicode "Unicode"), the [code point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Code_point "Code point") for "bicycle" is U+1F6B2. The [entity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numeric_character_reference "Numeric character reference")`🚲` in [HTML](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTML "HTML") produces 🚲.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-13)

## History

This section is an excerpt from [History of the bicycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_bicycle "History of the bicycle").[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_the_bicycle&action=edit)]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5d/1886_Swift_Safety_Bicycle_Coventry_Transport_Museum.jpg/330px-1886_Swift_Safety_Bicycle_Coventry_Transport_Museum.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1886_Swift_Safety_Bicycle_Coventry_Transport_Museum.jpg)

1886 Swift Safety Bicycle

The "[dandy horse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dandy_horse "Dandy horse")",[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-14) also called _Draisienne_ or _Laufmaschine_ ("running machine"), was the first human means of transport to use only two wheels in [tandem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tandem "Tandem") and was invented by the German [Baron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freiherr "Freiherr")[Karl von Drais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Drais "Karl Drais"). It is regarded as the first bicycle and von Drais is seen as the "father of the bicycle",[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-History_of_the_bicycle_:0-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-History_of_the_bicycle_:1-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-History_of_the_bicycle_:2-17) but it did not have pedals.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-20) Von Drais introduced it to the public in [Mannheim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mannheim "Mannheim") in 1817 and in Paris in 1818.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-History_of_the_bicycle_csts-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHerlihy200426-22) The rider sat astride a wooden frame supported by two in-line wheels and pushed the vehicle along with their feet while steering the front wheel.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-History_of_the_bicycle_csts-21)

The [first mechanically propelled, two-wheeled vehicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treadle_bicycle "Treadle bicycle") may have been built by [Kirkpatrick MacMillan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirkpatrick_MacMillan "Kirkpatrick MacMillan"), a Scottish blacksmith, in 1839, although this claim is often disputed.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHerlihy200466%E2%80%9367-23) He is also associated with the first recorded instance of a cycling traffic offense, when a Glasgow newspaper in 1842 reported an accident in which an anonymous "gentleman from Dumfries-shire... bestride a velocipede... of ingenious design" knocked over a little girl in Glasgow and was fined five [shillings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shilling "Shilling") (equivalent to £24 in 2025).[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-24)

In the early 1860s, the Frenchmen [Pierre Michaux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Michaux "Pierre Michaux") and [Pierre Lallement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Lallement "Pierre Lallement") took bicycle design in a new direction by adding a mechanical [crank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crank_(mechanism) "Crank (mechanism)") drive with pedals on an enlarged front wheel (the [velocipede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velocipede "Velocipede")). This was the first in mass production. Another French inventor named Douglas Grasso had a failed prototype of Pierre Lallement's bicycle several years earlier. Several inventions followed using rear-wheel drive, the best known being the rod-driven velocipede by Scotsman [Thomas McCall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_McCall_(inventor) "Thomas McCall (inventor)") in 1869. In the same year, bicycle wheels with wire spokes were patented by [Eugène Meyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eug%C3%A8ne_Meyer_(inventor) "Eugène Meyer (inventor)") of Paris.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-25) The French _vélocipède_, made of iron and wood, developed into the "[penny-farthing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny-farthing "Penny-farthing")" (historically known as an "ordinary bicycle", a [retronym](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retronym "Retronym"), since there was then no other kind).[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-FOOTNOTENorcliffe200150-26) It featured a tubular steel frame on which were mounted wire-spoked wheels with solid rubber tires. These bicycles were difficult to mount, dismount and brake due to their high seat over the large front wheel. In 1868, Rowley Turner, a sales agent of the Coventry Sewing Machine Company (which soon became the [Coventry Machinists Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillman#History "Hillman")), brought a Michaux cycle to [Coventry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coventry "Coventry"), England. His uncle, Josiah Turner, and business partner [James Starley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Starley "James Starley"), used this as a basis for the 'Coventry Model' in what became Britain's first cycle factory.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-27)

The _dwarf ordinary_ addressed some of these faults by reducing the front wheel [diameter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diameter "Diameter") and setting the [seat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_seat "Bicycle seat") further back. This, in turn, required gearing—effected in a variety of ways—to efficiently use pedal power. Having to both pedal and steer via the front wheel remained a problem. Englishman [J.K. Starley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kemp_Starley "John Kemp Starley") (nephew of James Starley), J.H. Lawson, and Shergold solved this problem by introducing the [chain drive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chain_drive "Chain drive") (originated by the unsuccessful "bicyclette" of Englishman Henry Lawson),[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-FOOTNOTENorcliffe200147-28) connecting the frame-mounted cranks to the rear wheel. These models were known as [safety bicycles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safety_bicycle "Safety bicycle"), dwarf safeties, or upright bicycles for their lower seat height. Although, without pneumatic tires, the ride of the smaller-wheeled bicycle would be much rougher than that of the larger-wheeled variety. Starley's 1885 [Rover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rover_Company "Rover Company"), manufactured in Coventry[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-29) is usually described as the first recognizably modern bicycle.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-30) Soon, the _seat tube_ was added, which created the modern bike's double-triangle _diamond frame_.

Further innovations increased comfort and ushered in a second [bicycle craze](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_craze "Bicycle craze"), the 1890s _Golden Age of Bicycles_. In 1888, Scotsman [John Boyd Dunlop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Boyd_Dunlop "John Boyd Dunlop") introduced the first practical pneumatic tire, which soon became universal. [Willie Hume](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Hume "Willie Hume") demonstrated the supremacy of Dunlop's tyres in 1889, winning the tyre's first-ever races in Ireland and then England.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-History_of_the_bicycle_Gold_Hume-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-History_of_the_bicycle_Dunlop_time-32) Soon after, the rear [freewheel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freewheel "Freewheel") was developed, enabling the rider to coast. This refinement led to the 1890s invention[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-33) of [coaster brakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coaster_brake "Coaster brake"). [Derailleur gears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derailleur_gears "Derailleur gears") and hand-operated [Bowden cable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowden_cable "Bowden cable")-pull brakes were also developed during these years, but were only slowly adopted by casual riders.

The [Svea Velocipede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Svea_Velocipede "Svea Velocipede") with vertical pedal arrangement and [locking hubs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locking_hubs "Locking hubs") was introduced in 1892 by the Swedish engineers [Fredrik Ljungström](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredrik_Ljungstr%C3%B6m "Fredrik Ljungström") and [Birger Ljungström](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birger_Ljungstr%C3%B6m "Birger Ljungström").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-34)

In the 1870s, many [cycling clubs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_club "Cycling club") flourished. They were popular in a time when there were no cars on the market and the principal mode of transportation was [horse-drawn vehicles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horse-drawn_vehicle "Horse-drawn vehicle"). Among the earliest clubs was [The Bicycle Touring Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_UK "Cycling UK"), which has operated since 1878. By the turn of the century, cycling clubs flourished on both sides of the Atlantic, and touring and racing became widely popular. The [Raleigh Bicycle Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raleigh_Bicycle_Company "Raleigh Bicycle Company") was founded in [Nottingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nottingham "Nottingham"), England in 1888. It became the biggest bicycle manufacturer in the world, making over two million bikes per year.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-35)

Bicycles and [horse buggies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buggy_(carriage) "Buggy (carriage)") were the two mainstays of private transportation just prior to the automobile, and the grading of smooth roads in the late 19th century was stimulated by the widespread advertising, production, and use of these devices.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHerlihy2004280-5) More than 1 billion bicycles had been manufactured worldwide by the early 21st century.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-History_of_the_bicycle_Koeppel2007-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-History_of_the_bicycle_Economist2011-37) Bicycles are the most common vehicle of any kind in the world, and the most numerous model of any kind of vehicle, whether human-powered or [motor vehicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motor_vehicle "Motor vehicle"), is the Chinese [Flying Pigeon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flying_Pigeon "Flying Pigeon"), with numbers exceeding 500 million.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-History_of_the_bicycle_Koeppel2007-36)

## Uses

Main article: [Cycling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling "Cycling")

Bicycles are used for transportation, [bicycle commuting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_commuting "Bicycle commuting"), and [utility cycling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utility_cycling "Utility cycling").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-38)[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_] The [energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy "Energy") taken to cycle to a particular distance takes less than the energy to [walk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walking "Walking") as far by four-fifths or 80 percent.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilson197382-39) They are also used professionally by [mail carriers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_mail "Bicycle mail"), [paramedics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramedic "Paramedic"), [police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police_bicycle "Police bicycle"), [messengers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_messenger "Bicycle messenger"), and [for deliveries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cargo_bike "Cargo bike"). Military uses of bicycles included [communications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_communications "Military communications"), [reconnaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconnaissance "Reconnaissance"), troop movement, supply of provisions, and patrol, such as in [bicycle infantries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_infantry "Bicycle infantry").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-40)

They are also used for fun, including [bicycle touring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_touring "Bicycle touring"), [mountain biking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain_biking "Mountain biking"), [physical fitness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physical_fitness "Physical fitness"), and [play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Play_(activity) "Play (activity)"). [Bicycle sports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycle_sport "Cycle sport") include [racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_bicycle_racing "Road bicycle racing"), [BMX racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BMX_racing "BMX racing"), [track racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Track_cycling "Track cycling"), [criterium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criterium "Criterium"), [roller racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_rollers "Bicycle rollers"), [sportives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclosportive "Cyclosportive") and [time trials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_trial "Time trial"). They are also used for entertainment and pleasure in other ways, such as in organised mass rides, [artistic cycling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artistic_cycling "Artistic cycling") and [freestyle BMX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freestyle_BMX "Freestyle BMX").

The more common types include [utility bicycles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utility_bicycle "Utility bicycle"), [mountain bicycles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain_bicycle "Mountain bicycle"), [racing bicycles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racing_bicycle "Racing bicycle"), [touring bicycles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Touring_bicycle "Touring bicycle"), [hybrid bicycles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hybrid_bicycle "Hybrid bicycle"), [cruiser bicycles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cruiser_bicycle "Cruiser bicycle"),[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_][BMX bikes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BMX_bike "BMX bike") and [electric bicycles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_bicycles "Electric bicycles"). ### Dynamics

Main article: [Bicycle and motorcycle dynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_and_motorcycle_dynamics "Bicycle and motorcycle dynamics")

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1b/Jersey_Town_Criterium_2011_81.jpg/250px-Jersey_Town_Criterium_2011_81.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jersey_Town_Criterium_2011_81.jpg)

A cyclist leaning in a turn

A bicycle stays upright while moving forward by being steered so as to keep its [center of mass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_of_mass "Center of mass") over the wheels, that is in line with the resultant force of gravity and centrifugal force.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-NS2581-45) This steering is usually provided by the rider, but under certain conditions, may be provided by the bicycle itself.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-MPRS-46)

The combined center of mass of a bicycle and its rider must lean into a turn. This lean is induced by a method known as [countersteering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Countersteering "Countersteering"), which can be performed by the rider turning the handlebars directly with the hands[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-Wilson-47) or indirectly by leaning the bicycle.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-fajans-48)

Short-wheelbase or tall bicycles, when braking, can generate enough stopping force at the front wheel to flip longitudinally.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-49) The act of purposefully using this force to lift the rear wheel and balance on the front without tipping over is a trick known as a [stoppie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoppie "Stoppie"), endo, or front wheelie.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-50)

### Performance

Main article: [Bicycle performance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_performance "Bicycle performance")

The bicycle is extraordinarily efficient in both biological and mechanical terms. The bicycle is the most efficient human-powered means of transportation in terms of energy a person must expend to travel a given distance, when travelling slowly or equipped with an aerodynamic fairing. From a mechanical viewpoint, up to 99% of the energy delivered by the rider into the pedals is transmitted to the wheels, although the use of gearing mechanisms may reduce this by 10–15% and there is also a small amount of tire slip.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-whitt-52)

A human traveling on a bicycle at low to medium speeds of about 16–24 km/h (10–15 mph) uses only the power required to walk. Air drag, which is proportional to the square of speed, requires dramatically higher power outputs as speeds increase. If the rider is sitting upright, the rider's body creates about 75% of the total drag of the bicycle/rider combination. Drag can be reduced by seating the rider in a more [aerodynamically](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerodynamic "Aerodynamic") streamlined position. Drag can also be reduced by covering the bicycle with an aerodynamic [fairing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_fairing "Bicycle fairing"). The fastest recorded unpaced speed on a flat surface with a standing start was the hour record in 2016: over 92 km/h (57 mph) with a highly streamlined bicycle.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-53)

### Frame

Main article: [Bicycle frame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_frame "Bicycle frame")

Most modern bicycles have a frame with upright seating that looks much like the first chain-driven bike.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHerlihy2004200%E2%80%9350-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHerlihy2004266%E2%80%9371-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHerlihy2004280-5) These upright bicycles frequently have a _diamond frame_, a [truss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truss "Truss") consisting of two triangles: the front triangle and the rear triangle. The front triangle consists of the top tube and down tube (connected by the head tube), and seat tube. The head tube contains the [headset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Headset_(bicycle_part) "Headset (bicycle part)"), the set of bearings that allows the [fork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_fork "Bicycle fork") to turn smoothly for steering and balance. The rear triangle consists of the seat tube, with the [bottom bracket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bottom_bracket "Bottom bracket") at the bottom, and paired _chain stays_ and _seat stays_, connecting at the rear [dropouts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fork_end "Fork end"), where the axle for the rear wheel is held.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-55) The frame's shape allows the rider's weight to be distributed in a way that does not misshapen or compress the entire frame as it turns.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilson197385-56)

Historically, women's bicycle frames had a top tube that connected in the middle of the seat tube instead of the top, resulting in a lower [standover height](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frame_geometry "Frame geometry") at the expense of compromised structural integrity, since this places a strong bending load in the seat tube, and bicycle frame members are typically weak in bending. This design, referred to as a _[step-through frame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Step-through\_frame "Step-through frame")_ or as an _open frame_, allows the rider to mount and dismount in a dignified way while wearing a skirt or dress. While some women's bicycles continue to use this frame style, there is also a variation, the _[mixte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixte "Mixte")_, which splits the top tube laterally into two thinner top tubes that bypass the seat tube on each side and connect to the rear fork ends.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-57)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-59)

Another style is the [recumbent bicycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recumbent_bicycle "Recumbent bicycle"). These are inherently more aerodynamic than upright versions, as the rider may lean back onto a support and operate pedals that are on about the same level as the seat. The world's fastest bicycle is a recumbent bicycle but this type was banned from competition in 1934 by the [Union Cycliste Internationale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Cycliste_Internationale "Union Cycliste Internationale").[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-60)

Historically, materials used in bicycles have followed a similar pattern as in aircraft, the goal being high strength and low weight. Since the late 1930s, alloy steels have been used for frame and fork tubes in higher quality machines. By the 1980s, [aluminum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminum "Aluminum")[welding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welding "Welding") techniques had improved to the point that aluminum tube could safely be used instead of [steel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steel "Steel"). Since then aluminum alloy frames and other components have become popular due to their light weight, and most mid-range bikes are now aluminum alloy. More expensive bikes sometimes use [titanium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titanium "Titanium") or more often [carbon fibre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_fibre "Carbon fibre") laid-up in resin due to its significantly lighter weight and profiling ability, allowing designers to make a bike both stiff and compliant by arranging the angles of the laid-up fibres optimally. Virtually all professional racing bicycles now use carbon fibre frames, as they have the best strength to weight ratio. A typical modern carbon fiber frame can weigh less than 2 pounds (1 kg).[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-61)

Wood and [bamboo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bamboo "Bamboo"), a natural [composite material](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Composite_material "Composite material") with high strength-to-weight ratio and [stiffness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stiffness "Stiffness"),[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-Lakkad-62) have been used for bicycles since 1894.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-lukenbill-63) Modern versions use bamboo for the primary frame with glued metal connections and parts.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-lukenbill-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-65)

### Drivetrain and gearing

Main article: [Bicycle drivetrain systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_drivetrain_systems "Bicycle drivetrain systems")

The _drivetrain_ begins with pedals which rotate the [cranks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crank_set "Crank set"), which are held in axis by the bottom bracket. Most bicycles use a chain to transmit power to the rear wheel. A very small number of bicycles use a shaft drive to transmit power. Hydraulic bicycle transmissions have been built, but they can be inefficient and complex.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-:0-66)

Since cyclists' legs are most efficient over a narrow range of pedaling speeds, or [cadence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cadence_(cycling) "Cadence (cycling)"), a variable [gear ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gear_ratio "Gear ratio") helps a cyclist to maintain an optimum pedalling speed while covering varied terrain. Some, mainly utility, bicycles use [hub gears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hub_gear "Hub gear") with between 3 and 14 ratios, but most use the generally more efficient [derailleur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derailleur "Derailleur") system, by which the chain is moved between different cogs called chainrings and sprockets to select a ratio. A derailleur system normally has two derailleurs, or mechs, one at the front to select the [chainring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chainring "Chainring") and another at the back to select the sprocket. Most bikes have two or three chainrings, and from 5 to 12 sprockets on the back, with the number of theoretical gears calculated by multiplying front by back. In reality, many gears overlap or require the chain to run diagonally, so the number of usable gears is fewer.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-:0-66)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-67)

An alternative to chain drive is to use a toothed belt. These work much the same as a chain, they are popular with commuters as they require little maintenance. They are slightly less efficient than chains and cannot be shifted across a cassette of sprockets, and are used either as single speed or with a hub gear.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-:1-68)

[Different gears and ranges of gears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_gearing "Bicycle gearing") are appropriate for different people and styles of cycling. Multi-speed bicycles allow gear selection to suit the circumstances: a cyclist could use a high gear when cycling downhill, a medium gear when cycling on a flat road, and a low gear when cycling uphill. In a lower gear, every turn of the pedals leads to fewer rotations of the rear wheel. This allows the energy required to move the same distance to be distributed over more pedal turns, reducing fatigue when riding uphill, with a heavy load, or against strong winds. A higher gear allows a cyclist to make fewer pedal turns to maintain a given speed, but with more effort per turn of the pedals.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bike#cite_note-69)

With a _chain drive_ transmission, a _chainring_ attached to a crank drives the chain, which in turn rotates the rear wheel via the rear sprocket(s) ([cassette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassette_(bicycle_part) "Cassette (bicycle part)") or [freewheel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cogset#Freewheels "Cogset")). There are four gearing options: two-speed hub gear integrated with chain ring, up to 3 chain rings, up to 12 sprockets and hub gear built into rear wheel (3-speed to 14-speed). The most common options are either a rear hub or multiple chain rings combined with multiple sprockets (other combinations of options are possible but less common).
