**Marco Pantani** (Italian:[[ˈmarko panˈtaːni]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Italian "Help:IPA/Italian"); 13 January 1970 – 14 February 2004) was an Italian [road racing cyclist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_racing_cyclist "Road racing cyclist"), widely regarded as one of the greatest [climbing specialists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climbing_specialist "Climbing specialist") in the history of the sport by measures of his legacy, credits from other riders, and records. He recorded the fastest climbs up the Tour's iconic venues of Mont Ventoux (46:00)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-4) and Alpe d'Huez (36:50),[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-5) and other cyclists including [Lance Armstrong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lance_Armstrong "Lance Armstrong") and [Charly Gaul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charly_Gaul "Charly Gaul") have hailed Pantani's climbing skills.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-7) He is the second to last rider and one of only eight to ever win the [Tour de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tour_de_France "Tour de France") – [Giro d'Italia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giro_d'Italia "Giro d'Italia") double, doing so in 1998. He is the sixth of seven Italians, after [Ottavio Bottecchia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottavio_Bottecchia "Ottavio Bottecchia"), [Gino Bartali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gino_Bartali "Gino Bartali"), [Fausto Coppi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fausto_Coppi "Fausto Coppi"), [Gastone Nencini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gastone_Nencini "Gastone Nencini") and [Felice Gimondi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felice_Gimondi "Felice Gimondi"), and before [Vincenzo Nibali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincenzo_Nibali "Vincenzo Nibali") to win the Tour de France.

Pantani's cycling style was off-the-saddle, and was a relentless climbing style. His early death caused by acute [cocaine poisoning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cocaine_poisoning "Cocaine poisoning") in 2004 has further turned the cyclist into a popular icon. The narrative was cultivated by Pantani, who picked the nickname **"Il Pirata"** (English: "The Pirate") because of his shaven head and the [bandana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerchief "Kerchief") and earrings he wore.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-pantani_death-8) At 172 centimetres (5 feet 7+1⁄2 inches) and 58 kilograms (128 pounds), he was said to have the classic build for a [mountain climber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climbing_specialist "Climbing specialist").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-Gaul-3) His style has been contrasted with that of [time-trialling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Individual_time_trial "Individual time trial") experts such as the five-time Tour winner [Miguel Induráin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Indur%C3%A1in "Miguel Induráin").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-9)

Although Pantani never tested positive during his career, his career was beset by doping allegations. In the [1999 Giro d'Italia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_Giro_d'Italia "1999 Giro d'Italia"), he was expelled due to his irregular blood values. Although he was disqualified for "health reasons", it was implied that Pantani's high [haematocrit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haematocrit "Haematocrit") was the product of [EPO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erythropoietin "Erythropoietin") use. Following later accusations, Pantani went into a severe depression from which he never fully recovered, ultimately leading to his death in 2004.

## Early life and amateur career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Marco_Pantani&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and amateur career")]

Pantani was born on 13 January 1970 in [Cesena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesena "Cesena"), [Romagna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romagna "Romagna"), the son of Ferdinando (referred to as Paolo) and Tonina.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFoot2011265-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-11) He joined the Fausto Coppi cycling club of [Cesenatico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesenatico "Cesenatico") at the age of eleven.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFoot2011265-10)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-12) As an amateur, he won the 1992 [Girobio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girobio "Girobio"), the amateur version of the [Giro d'Italia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giro_d'Italia "Giro d'Italia"), after finishing third in 1990 and second in 1991.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-pantani_death-8)

## Professional career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Marco_Pantani&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Professional career")]

### 1992–1996: Early years

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Marco_Pantani&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1992–1996: Early years")]

His success at the Girobio led to his turning professional for the remainder of the 1992 season with [Davide Boifava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davide_Boifava "Davide Boifava")'s [Carrera Jeans–Vagabond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carrera_(cycling_team) "Carrera (cycling team)"). While signing the contract, barely above the minimum established, he asked Boifava what would happen if he were to win the [Giro d'Italia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giro_d'Italia "Giro d'Italia") or the [Tour de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tour_de_France "Tour de France"), requesting a change in the contract.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-loccidentale-13) He finished 12th in his first professional race, the [Gran Premio Città di Camaiore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gran_Premio_Citt%C3%A0_di_Camaiore "Gran Premio Città di Camaiore"). In 1993, his first full season as a professional, he finished fifth at the mountainous course of [Giro del Trentino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giro_del_Trentino "Giro del Trentino") and debuted at the [Giro d'Italia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993_Giro_d'Italia "1993 Giro d'Italia") in order to help his team leader, [Claudio Chiappucci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claudio_Chiappucci "Claudio Chiappucci"). He was forced to abandon the race in the 18th stage due to [tendinitis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tendinitis "Tendinitis").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-Wilcockson-14)

In 1994, he finished fourth at the [Giro del Trentino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giro_del_Trentino "Giro del Trentino") and the [Giro di Toscana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giro_di_Toscana "Giro di Toscana") before his second participation at the [Giro d'Italia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_Giro_d'Italia "1994 Giro d'Italia"), where he was supposed to help Chiappucci.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-Wilcockson-14) He won two consecutive mountain stages, earning his first victory as a professional in the fourteenth stage to [Merano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merano "Merano"). In the following stage to [Aprica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aprica "Aprica"), which featured the renowned [Stelvio Pass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stelvio_Pass "Stelvio Pass") and the [Mortirolo Pass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortirolo_Pass "Mortirolo Pass"), Pantani attacked at the base of Mortirolo and broke free at the Valico di Santa Cristina to win the stage at Aprica and place second in the overall classification.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-Wilcockson-14) He ultimately finished the race behind [Eugeni Berzin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugeni_Berzin "Eugeni Berzin") but ahead of [Miguel Induráin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Indur%C3%A1in "Miguel Induráin"), who had won the two previous Giros. That same year Pantani made his [Tour de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tour_de_France "Tour de France") debut, coming in third and winning the [young rider classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young_rider_classification_in_the_Tour_de_France "Young rider classification in the Tour de France") along the way. In 1995, he was hit by a car while training, preventing him from riding the Giro, but he rode the [Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_Tour_de_France "1995 Tour de France") and won stages at [Alpe d'Huez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpe_d'Huez "Alpe d'Huez") and [Guzet-Neige](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guzet-Neige "Guzet-Neige"). He also finished thirteenth and claimed his second successive best young rider prize. He also won a stage at the [Tour de Suisse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tour_de_Suisse "Tour de Suisse") and finished third in the [1995 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_UCI_Road_World_Championships "1995 UCI Road World Championships") road race in [Duitama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duitama "Duitama"), Colombia, behind Spaniards [Abraham Olano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Olano "Abraham Olano") and [Miguel Induráin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Indur%C3%A1in "Miguel Induráin"). Shortly after returning to Italy, he collided head-on with a car during the Italian [Milano–Torino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milano%E2%80%93Torino "Milano–Torino") race, sustaining multiple fractures to the left [tibia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibia "Tibia") and [fibula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibula "Fibula"),[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-PANT1-15) injuries that threatened his career and forced him to miss most of the 1996 season.

### 1997: Move to Mercatone Uno

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Marco_Pantani&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 1997: Move to Mercatone Uno")]

When Carrera Jeans manufacturers stopped sponsoring the Italian cycling team [Carrera Jeans–Tassoni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carrera_(cycling_team) "Carrera (cycling team)") at the end of 1996, a new team based in Italy was formed with Marco Pantani as the team leader. [Luciano Pezzi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pezzi "Luciano Pezzi") founded [Mercatone Uno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercatone_Uno%E2%80%93Scanavino "Mercatone Uno–Scanavino"), taking with him as [directeur sportifs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directeur_sportif "Directeur sportif")[Giuseppe Martinelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Martinelli "Giuseppe Martinelli"), [Davide Cassani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davide_Cassani "Davide Cassani") and Alessandro Giannelli and ten of the riders from Carrera.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-16) Pantani returned to the Giro in 1997, but he was injured when a black cat caused an accident in front of him during one of the first stages.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-17) Even though he completed the stage, he was treated at a hospital for a muscle injury in the same leg he had hurt in 1995.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-18) He returned to action at the [1997 Tour de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_Tour_de_France "1997 Tour de France") and won two stages in the [Alps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alps "Alps"), establishing a record time for the climb of [Alpe d'Huez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpe_d'Huez "Alpe d'Huez") and winning two days later at [Morzine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morzine "Morzine"). Jan Ullrich won, with Pantani third behind [Richard Virenque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Virenque "Richard Virenque").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcGannMcGann2008242-19) In 1997, Pantani rode the final 14.5 km to L`Alpe d`Huez in 37'35" minutes, which is the record to this day based on 14.5 km. Since the actual climb is just 13.8 km long, Pantani's time in 1997 was 36'55" minutes based on 13.8 km. His personal record for 13.8 km was in 1995, when he rode the climb in 36'40", which remained the fastest ascent time until [Tadej Pogačar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tadej_Poga%C4%8Dar "Tadej Pogačar") broke his record in the [2026 Tour de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Tour_de_France "2026 Tour de France") with a time of 35'27".[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-20) Pantani also still holds the third and fourth fastest times at 36'55" in 1997 and 37'15" in 1994, followed by [Lance Armstrong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lance_Armstrong "Lance Armstrong") at 37'36" in 2004 and [Jan Ullrich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Ullrich "Jan Ullrich") at 37'41" in 1997.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-21)

### 1998: Giro and Tour wins

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Marco_Pantani&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 1998: Giro and Tour wins")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ad/Pantani_Bike_1998_TdF.jpg/250px-Pantani_Bike_1998_TdF.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pantani_Bike_1998_TdF.jpg)

Bike used by Pantani during the [1998 Tour de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_Tour_de_France "1998 Tour de France")

In 1998, Pantani was considered a favorite to win the [Giro d'Italia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_Giro_d'Italia "1998 Giro d'Italia"). Other contenders included [Alex Zülle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Z%C3%BClle "Alex Zülle"), [1996](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_Giro_d'Italia "1996 Giro d'Italia") winner [Pavel Tonkov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pavel_Tonkov "Pavel Tonkov") and [1997](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_Giro_d'Italia "1997 Giro d'Italia") winner [Ivan Gotti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Gotti "Ivan Gotti").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-22) Zülle won the initial [prologue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Individual_time_trial "Individual time trial") in Nice and also won the sixth stage to [Lago Laceno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laceno "Laceno"), but Pantani recovered some time in the mountain stage to [Piancavallo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piancavallo "Piancavallo"). Pantani lost further time to his main rivals during the fifteenth stage, an individual time trial in [Trieste](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trieste "Trieste"). By that point, Pantani faced a disadvantage of almost four minutes to Zülle before the [Dolomites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolomites "Dolomites") mountain stages and an individual time trial on the penultimate stage, a discipline that favored Zülle and Tonkov. In the seventeenth stage to [Selva di Val Gardena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Val_Gardena "Val Gardena"), Pantani took the [maglia rosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_classification_in_the_Giro_d'Italia "General classification in the Giro d'Italia"), the leader's jersey, for the first time in his career after attacking Zülle on the [Marmolada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passo_Fedaia "Passo Fedaia") climb.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-cyclesport-23) Although Pantani crossed the finish line behind [Giuseppe Guerini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Guerini "Giuseppe Guerini"), he finished over four minutes ahead of Zülle, maintaining an advantage of thirty seconds on the general classification over Tonkov, thirty-one seconds on Guerini and over a minute on Zülle.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-24) In the following stage to [Alpe di Pampeago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpe_di_Pampeago "Alpe di Pampeago"), he finished second behind Tonkov but maintained the general classification lead over him and gained further time on Zülle and Guerini.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-25) In the eighteenth stage to [Plan di Montecampione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montecampione "Montecampione"), he repeatedly attacked Tonkov, dropping him in the last three kilometers and winning the stage to face the individual time trial on the penultimate stage with a lead of almost a minute and a half.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-cyclesport-23) Zülle lost contact with the favorites in the first climb and ended up losing over thirty minutes.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-26) Having won over two minutes on Pantani in the previous time trial, Tonkov was considered superior to Pantani on the time trial discipline, but the Italian finished third in the penultimate stage, gaining an additional five seconds on Tonkov.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-27) Pantani was thus able to maintain his lead to win the Giro d'Italia with a minute and a half over Tonkov and more than six minutes over Guerini. He also won the [Mountains classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountains_classification_in_the_Giro_d'Italia "Mountains classification in the Giro d'Italia") and finished second in the [Points classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Points_classification_in_the_Giro_d'Italia "Points classification in the Giro d'Italia").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-28)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/0/0c/Pantani_graffito98.jpg/250px-Pantani_graffito98.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pantani_graffito98.jpg)

Fans on the roadside of the climb to Les Deux Alpes, awaiting the arrival of the [1998 Tour de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_Tour_de_France "1998 Tour de France")

In the [Tour de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_Tour_de_France "1998 Tour de France"), Pantani started the race by finishing 181st of 189 riders in the opening prologue, and losing over four minutes in the first [individual time trial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Individual_time_trial "Individual time trial") to [1997 Tour de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_Tour_de_France "1997 Tour de France") winner [Jan Ullrich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Ullrich "Jan Ullrich"). Pantani pulled back these early time losses to Ullrich, first in the [Pyrenees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenees "Pyrenees") by taking 23 seconds off Ullrich in the stage to [Luchon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bagn%C3%A8res-de-Luchon "Bagnères-de-Luchon")[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-29) and winning the stage to [Plateau de Beille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plateau_de_Beille "Plateau de Beille"), where he took an additional minute and forty seconds from Ullrich.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-30) Although he was still three minutes behind Ullrich after the Pyrenees, he defeated him by almost nine minutes in the first mountain stage in the [Alps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alps "Alps"), from [Grenoble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble "Grenoble") to [Les Deux Alpes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_Deux_Alpes "Les Deux Alpes"), via the [Col de la Croix de Fer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Col_de_la_Croix_de_Fer "Col de la Croix de Fer") and [Col du Galibier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Col_du_Galibier "Col du Galibier"). Pantani launched an attack on the ascent of Galibier, forty-eight kilometers from the finish. He stopped to put on a rain jacket at the summit to win on the final ascent to Deux Alpes.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-31) Pantani turned his three-minute deficit on Ullrich into a six-minute advantage that he maintained in the following stages to win the Tour de France ahead of [Jan Ullrich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Ullrich "Jan Ullrich") and [Bobby Julich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Julich "Bobby Julich"). Pantani became the first Italian since [Felice Gimondi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felice_Gimondi "Felice Gimondi") in 1965 to win the Tour and the seventh rider in history to achieve the [Giro-Tour double](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Tour_(cycling)#Winners_of_multiple_Grand_Tours_in_a_single_year "Grand Tour (cycling)"), a feat which no one had achieved since [Miguel Induráin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Indur%C3%A1in "Miguel Induráin") succeeded in 1993. Until [Tadej Pogacar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tadej_Pogacar "Tadej Pogacar") in 2024, Pantani was the last person to win the [Giro-Tour double](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Tour_(cycling)#Winners_of_multiple_Grand_Tours_in_a_single_year "Grand Tour (cycling)") in the same year. Following his success in the Tour, he stated that he may have won the cleanest Tour because of the fear of police following the [Festina affair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Festina_affair "Festina affair").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-32) Although he had just ended what would be his most successful season and he had always dreamed about winning the [yellow jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_classification_in_the_Tour_de_France "General classification in the Tour de France"), he later stated that he felt more alone than ever.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-loccidentale-13) French cycling magazine _Vélo Magazine_ awarded him the [Vélo d'Or](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V%C3%A9lo_d'Or "Vélo d'Or") as the best rider of 1998.

### 1999: Expelled at Madonna di Campiglio

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Marco_Pantani&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 1999: Expelled at Madonna di Campiglio")]

In 1999, Pantani started the season by winning a stage and the overall classification of [Vuelta a Murcia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vuelta_a_Murcia "Vuelta a Murcia") as well as a stage at the [Setmana Catalana de Ciclisme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Setmana_Catalana_de_Ciclisme "Setmana Catalana de Ciclisme"). Pantani was leading the [Giro d'Italia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_Giro_d'Italia "1999 Giro d'Italia"), with only one mountain stage left, when a blood test at [Madonna di Campiglio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madonna_di_Campiglio "Madonna di Campiglio") showed that he had a 52-per cent [hematocrit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hematocrit "Hematocrit") reading, above the 50-per cent upper limit set by [UCI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Cycliste_Internationale "Union Cycliste Internationale"). He was expelled from the race and forced to take a two-week break from racing, with no further action taken. Although the hematocrit test is officially branded as a "health check", a high reading suggests that a rider may have been [blood doping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blood_doping "Blood doping") with [EPO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erythropoietin "Erythropoietin").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDaunceyHare2003232-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-34) At the time of his disqualification, Pantani had won four stages and held a comfortable lead of five minutes and thirty-eight seconds over [Paolo Savoldelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paolo_Savoldelli "Paolo Savoldelli") and also led in the points and mountains classifications. As a result, the entire [Mercatone Uno–Bianchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercatone_Uno%E2%80%93Scanavino "Mercatone Uno–Scanavino") team withdrew from the race.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-35) Pantani stayed away from the rest of the year's races.

### 2000–2003: Late years

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Marco_Pantani&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 2000–2003: Late years")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/Pantani_briancon_2000_2.jpg/250px-Pantani_briancon_2000_2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pantani_briancon_2000_2.jpg)

Pantani near [Briançon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian%C3%A7on "Briançon") at the [2000 Tour de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Tour_de_France "2000 Tour de France")

In 2000, he was back in the Giro after deciding to ride only the day before the race started. He lost time and could not attack until the last mountain stage to [Briançon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian%C3%A7on "Briançon"), in which he helped his teammate [Stefano Garzelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stefano_Garzelli "Stefano Garzelli") to win. Pantani rode the [2000 Tour de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Tour_de_France "2000 Tour de France"). He was off the pace in the [Pyrenees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenees "Pyrenees"), but matched [Lance Armstrong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lance_Armstrong "Lance Armstrong") on [Mont Ventoux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mont_Ventoux "Mont Ventoux"), leaving the field behind. Armstrong eased and appeared to allow Pantani the stage victory. Pantani said that he felt insulted by the gesture, causing bad feelings between the two which were exacerbated when Armstrong referred to him as _Elefantino_ (Italian for "Little Elephant"), a reference to his prominent ears.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-36) In that same Tour, he won another stage, to [Courchevel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Courchevel "Courchevel"), that turned out to be his last victory as a professional. At that point, he was sixth in the overall classification, facing a disadvantage of nine minutes to Armstrong. On the next stage, which featured the [hors catégorie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hors_cat%C3%A9gorie "Hors catégorie")[Col de Joux-Plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Col_de_Joux-Plane "Col de Joux-Plane") to [Morzine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morzine "Morzine"), Pantani broke away with 120 km to go, trying to crush Armstrong, but he suffered stomach problems and withdrew the next day. He never raced the Tour again.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-37) Later in the year, he represented Italy in the [Sydney Olympics Road Race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycling_at_the_2000_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_road_race "Cycling at the 2000 Summer Olympics – Men's road race"), finishing 69th.

After that, he raced sporadically in 2001 and 2002, although he was demoralised from doping suspicions and had poor results. During the [2001 Giro d'Italia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Giro_d'Italia "2001 Giro d'Italia"), [Italian police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carabinieri "Carabinieri") raided the rooms of riders from all 20 teams and a syringe containing traces of [insulin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insulin "Insulin") was found in Pantani's room. He was banned for eight months by the [Italian Cycling Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federazione_Ciclistica_Italiana "Federazione Ciclistica Italiana") but later won an appeal due to an absence of proof.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-sanremo_insulin-38) In 2003, Pantani made another comeback in the [Giro d'Italia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_Giro_d'Italia "2003 Giro d'Italia"), finishing 14th overall. His best stage result was a fifth position after launching an unsuccessful attack on the slopes of [Monte Zoncolan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Zoncolan "Monte Zoncolan"),[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-39) while he launched his last attacks on the nineteenth stage to [Cascata del Toce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cascata_del_Toce "Cascata del Toce").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-40) It was the last time he rode a professional cycling race. After his team was not invited to the [2003 Tour de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_Tour_de_France "2003 Tour de France"), it was speculated that he would join [Bianchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bianchi_(cycling_team) "Bianchi (cycling team)") in order to ride the Tour, but he made a plea for privacy in late June following his admission to a psychiatric clinic which specialised in nervous disorders, drug addiction and alcoholism.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-41)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-42) After being released from the clinic, he was acquitted of a pending court case for sporting fraud regarding his blood values in [1999 Giro d'Italia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_Giro_d'Italia "1999 Giro d'Italia") because doping was not considered a crime in 1999. Pantani told an Italian newspaper that cycling fans had to forget about Pantani as an athlete, while stating that cycling was the last thing on his mind and that he had gained weight.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-1999_acquitted_bbc-43)

## Doping

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Marco_Pantani&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Doping")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8b/Tomb_of_Marco_Pantani.jpg/250px-Tomb_of_Marco_Pantani.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tomb_of_Marco_Pantani.jpg)

Tomb of Pantani in [Cesenatico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesenatico "Cesenatico"), Emilia-Romagna, Italy

After being disqualified at the [1999 Giro d'Italia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_Giro_d'Italia "1999 Giro d'Italia") for a [hematocrit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hematocrit "Hematocrit") reading of 52 per cent, above the 50-per cent upper limit set by [UCI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Cycliste_Internationale "Union Cycliste Internationale"), Pantani faced persistent allegations of doping throughout the rest of his career.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-1999_acquitted_bbc-43) Pantani has never been found using doping and has never been disqualified for doping.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-44)

The trial for the 1999 Giro d'Italia irregular blood values began in April 2003 and Pantani was eventually acquitted because doping was not considered a crime by the law at that time.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-PANT1-15) In early June 1999, a few days after Pantani was expelled from the 1999 Giro d'Italia, a court ordered the city of [Turin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turin "Turin") to compensate him for an accident in the 1995 edition of the [Milano–Torino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milano%E2%80%93Torino "Milano–Torino") that forced Pantani to undergo several surgeries and a long recovery to get back on his bike.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-45) A few days later, Italian prosecutor Raffaele Guariniello accused Pantani of a "sporting offence" after he discovered, by looking through trial and medical records, that Pantani's hematocrit after the accident was over 60 per cent.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-47)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-cyclingnews_oct_2000-48) Although the results did not surface until 1999, the [UCI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Cycliste_Internationale "Union Cycliste Internationale") had decided to implement blood testing in early 1997, imposing a 50-per cent upper limit for hematocrit. A rider with a value above 50 per cent was given a compulsory two-week suspension. The test was designated as a "health test", although it was administered on suspicion that the athlete was using the banned blood-boosting drug, [EPO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erythropoietin "Erythropoietin").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJeukendrup2002266-49)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJeukendrup2002310-50) During the proceeding, investigators tried to find a reason for Pantani's high hematocrit values, including an hematocrit value of 57.6% recorded on 1 May 1995, at a hospital after he had an accident while training, an investigation in which the doctor pointed out the presence of abnormal hematological values. Upon Guariniello's request to see Pantani's medical record after his accident at the [1997 Giro d'Italia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_Giro_d'Italia "1997 Giro d'Italia"), it was revealed that the blood test results had disappeared from the folder at the hospital and the police did not rule out "intentional removal".[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-52)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-53) Pantani was eventually indicted on a so-called "fraud in sport", but his lawyers argued that Pantani's hematocrit may have been elevated by a combination of training at high altitude in September, suffering from [dehydration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dehydration "Dehydration") during the race, [trauma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trauma_(medicine) "Trauma (medicine)") of his accident and a [margin of error](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margin_of_error "Margin of error") for the [sampling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sampling_(statistics) "Sampling (statistics)") method.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-cyclingnews_oct_2000-48) The original case started in Turin but was moved to [Forlì](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forl%C3%AC "Forlì") upon Pantani's lawyers' requests.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-54) Although he initially received a three-month [suspended sentence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suspended_sentence "Suspended sentence"),[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-55) Pantani's lawyers appealed and the case was dismissed in late 2001 because the law itself had been passed only in 1999.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-57)

In 1999, the Italian newspaper _[la Repubblica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La\_Repubblica "La Repubblica")_ published information that linked Pantani to an investigation on the use of performance-enhancing substances in Italian sports. According to the information released by the newspaper, [Francesco Conconi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_Conconi "Francesco Conconi") administered EPO to Italian athletes from 1993 to 1998, including Pantani and other cyclists of [Carrera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carrera_(cycling_team) "Carrera (cycling team)").[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-59) It was revealed that Pantani's name appeared on a file marked "Dblab", seized from Conconi's Biomedical Research Institute at [Ferrara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferrara "Ferrara"), which detailed athlete's hematocrit levels between 1993 and 1995. In 1994, his haematocrit values fluctuated from 40.7% on 16 March, early in the season, to 54.55% on 23 May, during the first stages of the [Giro d'Italia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_Giro_d'Italia "1994 Giro d'Italia"). His values reached 58% on 8 June, after winning two stages of the race, and were 57.4% on 27 July, after the [Tour de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_Tour_de_France "1994 Tour de France"). In March 1995, his hematocrit values had dropped to 45%, but they reached 56% in July during the [Tour de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_Tour_de_France "1995 Tour de France"), where he won two stages; and over 60% in October, after the accident in the Milano–Torino.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-61)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-62) In 2004, Conconi and his two assistants were acquitted by judge Franca Oliva because the actions were not deemed illegal at the time, although they were deemed "morally guilty" of promoting doping.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-64)

During the [2001 Giro d'Italia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Giro_d'Italia "2001 Giro d'Italia"), a syringe containing traces of [insulin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insulin "Insulin") was found in Pantani's room. Pantani claimed that the insulin had been [planted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/False_evidence "False evidence") and that he did not stay in the room that night.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-65) In 2002, he was banned for eight months by the [Italian Cycling Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federazione_Ciclistica_Italiana "Federazione Ciclistica Italiana"), but he later won an appeal due to an absence of proof.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-sanremo_insulin-38)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-66)

In 2006, two years after his death, Pantani was linked to the [Operación Puerto doping case](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operaci%C3%B3n_Puerto_doping_case "Operación Puerto doping case"). According to documentation released by Spanish radio network [Cadena SER](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cadena_SER "Cadena SER"), Pantani was allegedly given the code name "PTNI" by [Eufemiano Fuentes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eufemiano_Fuentes "Eufemiano Fuentes"), with a detailed program in 2003, his last season, including [EPO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erythropoietin "Erythropoietin"), [growth hormone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Growth_hormone "Growth hormone"), [Insulin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insulin "Insulin"), [Levothroid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levothroid "Levothroid") and [IGF-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insulin-like_growth_factor_1 "Insulin-like growth factor 1").[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-67) Italian newspaper _[Corriere della Sera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corriere\_della\_Sera "Corriere della Sera")_ indicated that he was administered over 40,000 units of EPO, seven doses of growth hormone, thirty doses of [anabolic steroids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anabolic_steroid "Anabolic steroid") and four doses of hormones used to treat menopause.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-68) In 2006, [Jesús Manzano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jes%C3%BAs_Manzano "Jesús Manzano"), a Spanish professional [road racing cyclist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_racing_cyclist "Road racing cyclist") whose statements led the [Guardia Civil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guardia_Civil "Guardia Civil") to conduct the Operación Puerto investigation, disclosed in an interview with French television channel [France 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France_3 "France 3") that Pantani was a client of Fuentes.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-69)

On the penultimate stage of [1998 Giro d'Italia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_Giro_d'Italia "1998 Giro d'Italia"), Pantani's teammate [Riccardo Forconi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riccardo_Forconi "Riccardo Forconi") was expelled from the race for an haematocrit value above 50 per cent. Ivano Fanini, the manager of [Amore & Vita–Giubileo 2000–Beretta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amore_&_Vita "Amore & Vita"), suggested during the early stages of 1999 Giro d'Italia that Pantani and Forconi had exchanged their blood samples in order to avoid Pantani's disqualification. According to Fanini, Forconi's haematocrit value was only 47 per cent the previous day.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-70) In 2008, Fanini further claimed that Forconi had received a house for the exchange but Forconi refuted these claims.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-71)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-72)

Matt Rendell's biography of Pantani suggests he used [recombinant erythropoietin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erythropoietin "Erythropoietin") (rEPO) throughout his professional career. It alleges that seasonal [hematocrit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hematocrit "Hematocrit") levels from several sources showed variations which exceeded those possible naturally, and that Pantani's main victories were probably won also thanks to blood hematocrit levels which could have been up to 60%.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-73)

A French senate report into doping released in July 2013 conjectured that Pantani, Jan Ullrich, Bobby Julich, Erik Zabel, Jacky Durand, and Laurent Desbiens had tested positive for EPO during retroactive testing of samples from the 1998 Tour de France conducted in 2004 but the tests aren't valid because the samples taken didn't conform to antidoping standards.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-74)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-75)

## Death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Marco_Pantani&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Death")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/f/f9/Marco_shrine.jpg/250px-Marco_shrine.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Marco_shrine.jpg)

Shrine to Pantani on the Mortirolo Pass erected by the Italian Professional Riders Association

In the early evening of 14 February 2004, Pantani was found dead at a hotel in [Rimini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rimini "Rimini"), Italy. An [autopsy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autopsy "Autopsy") revealed he had [cerebral edema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerebral_edema "Cerebral edema") and heart failure, and a coroner's [inquest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inquest "Inquest") revealed acute [cocaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cocaine "Cocaine") poisoning. Pantani spent the last days of his life isolated from his friends and family and barricaded himself inside his hotel room.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-76)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-77) Pantani's ex-girlfriend Christina Jonsson, in an April 2004 interview to Swiss news magazine _[L'Hebdo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L'Hebdo "L'Hebdo")_, indicated that following his expulsion from the [1999 Giro d'Italia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_Giro_d'Italia "1999 Giro d'Italia"), Pantani had confessed to her he had started using cocaine.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-78) In 2008, Fabio Carlino was convicted of supplying Pantani with a dose of ultra-pure cocaine that caused his death. The conviction was overturned in 2011 by the [Court of Cassation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Court_of_Cassation_(Italy) "Court of Cassation (Italy)") after the acting Prosecutor expressed doubts regarding the verdict, while stating that he "had the impression that the exaggerated media publicity surrounding Mr. Pantani's death led the judges to an excessive attribution of responsibility."[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-79) In 2016 the case was opened again,[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-80) but shelved, and then yet again; with Italian prosecutors citing about fifty pages of new evidence to consider, in November 2021.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-81)

Pantani was buried in his hometown, [Cesenatico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesenatico "Cesenatico"). Twenty thousand mourners were at his funeral, which was attended by [Franco Ballerini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franco_Ballerini "Franco Ballerini"), [Alberto Tomba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alberto_Tomba "Alberto Tomba"), [Azeglio Vicini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azeglio_Vicini "Azeglio Vicini"), [Mario Cipollini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario_Cipollini "Mario Cipollini") and [Diego Maradona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Maradona "Diego Maradona") among others.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-82) During the funeral, his manager Manuela Ronchi read notes that Pantani had written in his passport during a trip to Cuba:

> For four years I've been in every court, I just lost my desire to be like all the other sportsmen, but cycling has paid and many youngsters have lost their faith in justice. All my colleagues have been humiliated, with TV cameras hidden in their hotel rooms to try and ruin families. How could you not hurt yourself after that?[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-PANT1-15)[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-83)

[Miguel Induráin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Indur%C3%A1in "Miguel Induráin"), five-times [Tour de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tour_de_France "Tour de France") winner, praised Pantani by saying: "He got people hooked on the sport. There may be riders who have achieved more than him, but they never succeeded in drawing in the fans like he did."[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-84)

## Legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Marco_Pantani&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Legacy")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0f/Monumento_Pantani_Cesenatico.jpg/250px-Monumento_Pantani_Cesenatico.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Monumento_Pantani_Cesenatico.jpg)

Statue dedicated to Pantani at [Cesenatico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesenatico "Cesenatico")

In the years following his death, Pantani was the subject of several articles, books, songs and a film. Biographies and accounts on the life of Pantani have been written by sports journalists John Wilcockson and Matt Rendell, among others.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-85) Manuela Ronchi, Pantani's manager for five years, published an account on the last few years of Pantani's life titled _Man on the Run_.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-86) His mother Tonina Pantani also published a book in 2008 titled _\_Era mio figlio\__ (_He Was My Son_).[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-87) A [graphic novel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphic_novel "Graphic novel") titled _\_Gli ultimi giorni di Marco Pantani\__ (_The Last Days of Marco Pantani_) was released in 2011, chronicling the events that led up to Pantani's death. It was based on a book published by French journalist Philippe Brunel, a friend of Pantani, suggesting that Pantani may have been murdered.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-88) Italian television [RAI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAI "RAI") aired a television film in 2007 titled _[Il Pirata: Marco Pantani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Il\_Pirata:\_Marco\_Pantani "Il Pirata: Marco Pantani")_, a biographical film which starred [Rolando Ravello](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolando_Ravello "Rolando Ravello") as Marco Pantani.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-89) A documentary on Pantani's life titled _[Pantani: The Accidental Death of a Cyclist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantani:\_The\_Accidental\_Death\_of\_a\_Cyclist "Pantani: The Accidental Death of a Cyclist")_ was released in May 2014 in cinemas.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-90)

The [Memorial Marco Pantani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial_Marco_Pantani "Memorial Marco Pantani") has been organised annually since 2004 in his memory. The race starts in [Cesenatico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesenatico "Cesenatico"), Pantani's hometown, and follows a route towards his birthplace, [Cesena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesena "Cesena"). [Giro d'Italia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giro_d'Italia "Giro d'Italia")'s organisers decided to dedicate a mountain pass to Pantani's memory every year. In [the 2004 edition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Giro_d'Italia "2004 Giro d'Italia"), the first _Cima Pantani_ was [Mortirolo Pass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortirolo_Pass "Mortirolo Pass"), a mountain that played a key role in Pantani's history. When Mortirolo was included in the Giro for the third time in 1994, Pantani attacked and left everyone behind to earn a win at [Aprica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aprica "Aprica"). The 16th stage of [2004 Tour de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Tour_de_France "2004 Tour de France") was dedicated to Pantani's memory. This stage was an [individual time trial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Individual_time_trial "Individual time trial") up to [Alpe d'Huez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpe_d'Huez "Alpe d'Huez"), where Marco Pantani won in [1995](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_Tour_de_France "1995 Tour de France") and [1997](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_Tour_de_France "1997 Tour de France").[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-91)

A number of monuments and memorials have been erected in his honor at, among other places, [Mortirolo Pass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortirolo_Pass "Mortirolo Pass"),[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-92)[Colle Fauniera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colle_Fauniera "Colle Fauniera"),[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-93)[Col du Galibier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Col_du_Galibier "Col du Galibier"),[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-94) Poggio Murella in Tuscany where he had a house, and his hometown [Cesenatico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesenatico "Cesenatico").[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Pantani#cite_note-95)

**Cesenatico** ([Romagnol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romagnol_language "Romagnol language"): _Ziznàtic_) is a [port](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port "Port") town with about 26,000 inhabitants on the [Adriatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriatic_Sea "Adriatic Sea") coast of [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy"). It is located in the [province of Forlì-Cesena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Province_of_Forl%C3%AC-Cesena "Province of Forlì-Cesena") in the region of [Emilia-Romagna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emilia-Romagna "Emilia-Romagna"), about 30 kilometres (19 mi) south of [Ravenna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ravenna "Ravenna"). Cesenatico's port canal was surveyed and drawn by [Leonardo da Vinci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonardo_da_Vinci "Leonardo da Vinci") at the request of [Cesare Borgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesare_Borgia "Cesare Borgia"), as part of his plans to fortify the nearby town of [Cesena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesena "Cesena").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cesenatico&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Cesenatico was founded in 1302. It was considered part of the city of [Cesena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesena "Cesena") until it was incorporated at the beginning of the 18th century. Its port and canal were built in 1314,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesenatico#cite_note-4) with the canal originally planned to reach [Cesena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesena "Cesena"), some 15 kilometres (9 mi) inland. At the request of [Cesare Borgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesare_Borgia "Cesare Borgia") the canal was later surveyed by [Leonardo da Vinci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonardo_da_Vinci "Leonardo da Vinci"). It is often erroneously claimed that da Vinci designed the canal. In 1722 [James Francis Edward Stuart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Francis_Edward_Stuart "James Francis Edward Stuart") (the 'Old Pretender' to the British throne) stayed in Cesenatico's [Capuchin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_Friars_Minor_Capuchin "Order of Friars Minor Capuchin")[monastery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monastery "Monastery").

### 1860–present

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cesenatico&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: 1860–present")]

The Republican vocation of Cesenatico is evident in the elections of the following years, but this did not naturally prevent it from escaping fascism. The war damages were so enormous that it had to be rebuilt almost entirely. The municipal building, the aqueduct tower, the lighthouse, the pier and all the boats, the fish market, the schools as well as the villages of Villalta, Sala, Cannucceto, Villamarina, Bagnarola practically razed to the ground. The nightmare vanished on October 20, 1944, with the entry of the New Zealand allies.

The restoration and reconstruction work was immediately restarted. In 1945 the fishermen's cooperative was founded and a new impulse was given to the tourism that will lead Cesenatico to excel in this field. Many of the old "villas" were converted into hotels, new [colonies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonies "Colonies") were started (one of the first was the 12 Star Colony, aimed at children from the [autonomous province of Bolzano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autonomous_province_of_Bolzano "Autonomous province of Bolzano"), without language distinctions), and the construction of the famous [skyscraper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesenatico_Skyscraper "Cesenatico Skyscraper") gave launching a new era focused on mass tourism.

Today Cesenatico has about 22,000 hotel beds, with 3 million admissions per season. In 1966 the municipal library was founded; in the same year the coastal city was one of the first municipalities in Europe to start twinning projects with other cities. In 1977 a project of historical-archaeological recovery was brought to light and in the eighties the guidelines were introduced that launched Cesenatico from a global and European perspective.

## Monuments and places of interest

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cesenatico&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Monuments and places of interest")]

### Museums

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cesenatico&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Museums")]

*   Seafaring Museum: it is the most famous museum in the city and the only floating museum in Italy, which allows tourists to visit the most important moored ships, called "Bragozzo" and "Trabaccolo". Both boats had a transport and fishing version. The museum is located in the oldest part of the historical port-canal, which has a long maritime history behind it.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesenatico#cite_note-5)
*   Marino Moretti's house museum: Marino Moretti was a famous poet who was born in Cesenatico.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesenatico#cite_note-6)
*   Spazio Pantani: it is a structure directly managed by the Pantani family to keep alive the memory of the cycling champion Marco Pantani.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesenatico#cite_note-7)

### Municipal library

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cesenatico&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Municipal library")]

The municipal library, founded in 1966, is now located in a building of fascist era in Piazza Ciceruacchio. The book collections currently amount to about 60 000 books and the library has around 100 places for study, consultation and reading.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesenatico#cite_note-8)

### University

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cesenatico&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: University")]

Cesenatico hosts one of the seats of the Department of Veterinary Medical Sciences ([University of Bologna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bologna "University of Bologna")), for the bachelor's degree in "Aquaculture and Fish Production Hygiene".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesenatico#cite_note-9)

### Religious architecture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cesenatico&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Religious architecture")]

*   Parish church of San Giacomo Apostolo. Dating back to 1324, the current structure was defined in 1763, designed by [Pietro Bastoni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pietro_Bastoni "Pietro Bastoni"). Inside, there are some interesting works, among others by [Guido Cagnacci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guido_Cagnacci "Guido Cagnacci"). The external façade sees the historic boats of Leonardo's canal port.
*   Church of San Giuseppe.
*   Church of San Pietro Pescatore.
*   Church of the Capuchin friars, or Church of Saints Nicola di Mira and Francesco d'Assisi. It dates back to 1611, while the convent is three years later. Inside, there is a painting of [Saint Michael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Michael "Saint Michael") by the painter of [Forlì](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forl%C3%AC "Forlì") school [Gianfrancesco Modigliani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gianfrancesco_Modigliani?action=edit&redlink=1 "Gianfrancesco Modigliani (page does not exist)")[[it](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gianfrancesco%20Modigliani "it:Gianfrancesco Modigliani")].

## Society

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cesenatico&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Society")]

### Traditions and folklore

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cesenatico&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Traditions and folklore")]

From 1986 on the boats of the Maritime Museum the Nativity of the Marineria was set up. During the Christmas period, from the first Sunday of December until the Epiphany, the boats of the Floating Section of the Maritime Museum become the stage of the Marine Nativity Scene. The crib was born in 1986 and is the work of the artists Tinin Mantegazza, Maurizio Bertoni and Mino Savadori, from an original idea by Guerrino Gardini. The first sculpted statue was that of San Giacomo, patron saint of Cesenatico to whom many others have been added over the years. These are not just traditional statues that can be seen in the cribs, but glimpses inspired by the life of the common people of a fishing village: fishermen, carpenters, puppeteers.

Every year the crib is enriched with a new statue and a new character. From the seven figures with which they debuted in 1986 today the sculptural heritage is about fifty statues. This is how the project of the artists Bertoni and Savadori was carried out in order to equip each of the boats of a helmsman and a crewman over the years. The figures are thought of as elements of a representation, to be seen from the banks of the Leonardesco Canal Port as well as from an audience; illuminated, because in the crib are the lights that give life to the figures and mark the story.

## Main sights

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cesenatico&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Main sights")]

[![Image 12: house on a pier, with large nets hanging from long poles](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bd/Cesenatico_-_Canal_port_-_Fishing_house_%28Trabucco%29_2023-08-15.jpg/250px-Cesenatico_-_Canal_port_-_Fishing_house_%28Trabucco%29_2023-08-15.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cesenatico_-_Canal_port_-_Fishing_house_(Trabucco)_2023-08-15.jpg)

Fishing house or [trabucco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trabucco "Trabucco") on the canal port of Cesenatico

Today Cesenatico is a [tourist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism "Tourism") resort. It is home to the Museum of Seafaring ([Museo della Marineria di Cesenatico](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museo%20della%20marineria%20di%20Cesenatico "it:Museo della marineria di Cesenatico")), where historic fishing boats are displayed in the canal. There are also [trabucco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trabucco "Trabucco"), or fishing houses.

In the coastal city of Cesenatico, the port canal (in Italian [Porto Canale Leonardesco](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porto%20Canale%20Leonardesco "it:Porto Canale Leonardesco")) has always been the leading element of the historical city centre: it was the engine of the economy of the city, which relied on maritime trade and fishing and nowadays it is an outstanding point of interest for tourists, which are also attracted by the floating exhibit of the Museum of Seafaring.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesenatico#cite_note-10)

The town also features a 118-metre (387 ft) high [skyscraper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skyscraper "Skyscraper"), which for a few years was among the 30 highest buildings in Europe.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesenatico#cite_note-11)

## Events

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cesenatico&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Events")]

Cesenatico hosts every year the final stage of the [Italian Mathematics Olympiad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Mathematics_Olympiad?action=edit&redlink=1 "Italian Mathematics Olympiad (page does not exist)"), a mathematical _battle of wits_ between the best 300 high school students in Italy. It is usually held in the week-end following the first Thursday of May.

Cesenatico holds the Annual "Marco Pantani Nove Colli" cycling road event across nine of the Apennine foothills in May of each year. Other events associated include the Nove Colli Off Road and Junior Event in September each year.

**Cesenatico** ([Romagnol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romagnol_language "Romagnol language"): _Ziznàtic_) is a [port](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port "Port") town with about 26,000 inhabitants on the [Adriatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriatic_Sea "Adriatic Sea") coast of [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy"). It is located in the [province of Forlì-Cesena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Province_of_Forl%C3%AC-Cesena "Province of Forlì-Cesena") in the region of [Emilia-Romagna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emilia-Romagna "Emilia-Romagna"), about 30 kilometres (19 mi) south of [Ravenna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ravenna "Ravenna"). Cesenatico's port canal was surveyed and drawn by [Leonardo da Vinci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonardo_da_Vinci "Leonardo da Vinci") at the request of [Cesare Borgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesare_Borgia "Cesare Borgia"), as part of his plans to fortify the nearby town of [Cesena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesena "Cesena").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cesenatico&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Cesenatico was founded in 1302. It was considered part of the city of [Cesena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesena "Cesena") until it was incorporated at the beginning of the 18th century. Its port and canal were built in 1314,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesenatico#cite_note-4) with the canal originally planned to reach [Cesena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesena "Cesena"), some 15 kilometres (9 mi) inland. At the request of [Cesare Borgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesare_Borgia "Cesare Borgia") the canal was later surveyed by [Leonardo da Vinci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonardo_da_Vinci "Leonardo da Vinci"). It is often erroneously claimed that da Vinci designed the canal. In 1722 [James Francis Edward Stuart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Francis_Edward_Stuart "James Francis Edward Stuart") (the 'Old Pretender' to the British throne) stayed in Cesenatico's [Capuchin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_Friars_Minor_Capuchin "Order of Friars Minor Capuchin")[monastery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monastery "Monastery").

### 1860–present

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cesenatico&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: 1860–present")]

The Republican vocation of Cesenatico is evident in the elections of the following years, but this did not naturally prevent it from escaping fascism. The war damages were so enormous that it had to be rebuilt almost entirely. The municipal building, the aqueduct tower, the lighthouse, the pier and all the boats, the fish market, the schools as well as the villages of Villalta, Sala, Cannucceto, Villamarina, Bagnarola practically razed to the ground. The nightmare vanished on October 20, 1944, with the entry of the New Zealand allies.

The restoration and reconstruction work was immediately restarted. In 1945 the fishermen's cooperative was founded and a new impulse was given to the tourism that will lead Cesenatico to excel in this field. Many of the old "villas" were converted into hotels, new [colonies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonies "Colonies") were started (one of the first was the 12 Star Colony, aimed at children from the [autonomous province of Bolzano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autonomous_province_of_Bolzano "Autonomous province of Bolzano"), without language distinctions), and the construction of the famous [skyscraper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesenatico_Skyscraper "Cesenatico Skyscraper") gave launching a new era focused on mass tourism.

Today Cesenatico has about 22,000 hotel beds, with 3 million admissions per season. In 1966 the municipal library was founded; in the same year the coastal city was one of the first municipalities in Europe to start twinning projects with other cities. In 1977 a project of historical-archaeological recovery was brought to light and in the eighties the guidelines were introduced that launched Cesenatico from a global and European perspective.

## Monuments and places of interest

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cesenatico&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Monuments and places of interest")]

### Museums

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cesenatico&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Museums")]

*   Seafaring Museum: it is the most famous museum in the city and the only floating museum in Italy, which allows tourists to visit the most important moored ships, called "Bragozzo" and "Trabaccolo". Both boats had a transport and fishing version. The museum is located in the oldest part of the historical port-canal, which has a long maritime history behind it.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesenatico#cite_note-5)
*   Marino Moretti's house museum: Marino Moretti was a famous poet who was born in Cesenatico.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesenatico#cite_note-6)
*   Spazio Pantani: it is a structure directly managed by the Pantani family to keep alive the memory of the cycling champion Marco Pantani.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesenatico#cite_note-7)

### Municipal library

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cesenatico&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Municipal library")]

The municipal library, founded in 1966, is now located in a building of fascist era in Piazza Ciceruacchio. The book collections currently amount to about 60 000 books and the library has around 100 places for study, consultation and reading.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesenatico#cite_note-8)

### University

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cesenatico&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: University")]

Cesenatico hosts one of the seats of the Department of Veterinary Medical Sciences ([University of Bologna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bologna "University of Bologna")), for the bachelor's degree in "Aquaculture and Fish Production Hygiene".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesenatico#cite_note-9)

### Religious architecture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cesenatico&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Religious architecture")]

Inside, there are some interesting works, among others by [Guido Cagnacci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guido_Cagnacci "Guido Cagnacci"). The external façade sees the historic boats of Leonardo's canal port.

*   Church of the Capuchin friars, or Church of Saints Nicola di Mira and Francesco d'Assisi. It dates back to 1611, while the convent is three years later. ### Traditions and folklore

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cesenatico&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Traditions and folklore")]

From 1986 on the boats of the Maritime Museum the Nativity of the Marineria was set up. During the Christmas period, from the first Sunday of December until the Epiphany, the boats of the Floating Section of the Maritime Museum become the stage of the Marine Nativity Scene. The crib was born in 1986 and is the work of the artists Tinin Mantegazza, Maurizio Bertoni and Mino Savadori, from an original idea by Guerrino Gardini. The first sculpted statue was that of San Giacomo, patron saint of Cesenatico to whom many others have been added over the years. These are not just traditional statues that can be seen in the cribs, but glimpses inspired by the life of the common people of a fishing village: fishermen, carpenters, puppeteers.

Every year the crib is enriched with a new statue and a new character. From the seven figures with which they debuted in 1986 today the sculptural heritage is about fifty statues. This is how the project of the artists Bertoni and Savadori was carried out in order to equip each of the boats of a helmsman and a crewman over the years. The figures are thought of as elements of a representation, to be seen from the banks of the Leonardesco Canal Port as well as from an audience; illuminated, because in the crib are the lights that give life to the figures and mark the story.

## Main sights

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cesenatico&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Main sights")]

[![Image 12: house on a pier, with large nets hanging from long poles](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bd/Cesenatico_-_Canal_port_-_Fishing_house_%28Trabucco%29_2023-08-15.jpg/250px-Cesenatico_-_Canal_port_-_Fishing_house_%28Trabucco%29_2023-08-15.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cesenatico_-_Canal_port_-_Fishing_house_(Trabucco)_2023-08-15.jpg)

Fishing house or [trabucco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trabucco "Trabucco") on the canal port of Cesenatico

Today Cesenatico is a [tourist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism "Tourism") resort. It is home to the Museum of Seafaring ([Museo della Marineria di Cesenatico](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museo%20della%20marineria%20di%20Cesenatico "it:Museo della marineria di Cesenatico")), where historic fishing boats are displayed in the canal. There are also [trabucco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trabucco "Trabucco"), or fishing houses.

In the coastal city of Cesenatico, the port canal (in Italian [Porto Canale Leonardesco](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porto%20Canale%20Leonardesco "it:Porto Canale Leonardesco")) has always been the leading element of the historical city centre: it was the engine of the economy of the city, which relied on maritime trade and fishing and nowadays it is an outstanding point of interest for tourists, which are also attracted by the floating exhibit of the Museum of Seafaring.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesenatico#cite_note-10)

The town also features a 118-metre (387 ft) high [skyscraper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skyscraper "Skyscraper"), which for a few years was among the 30 highest buildings in Europe.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesenatico#cite_note-11)

## Events

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cesenatico&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Events")]

Cesenatico hosts every year the final stage of the [Italian Mathematics Olympiad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Mathematics_Olympiad?action=edit&redlink=1 "Italian Mathematics Olympiad (page does not exist)"), a mathematical _battle of wits_ between the best 300 high school students in Italy. It is usually held in the week-end following the first Thursday of May.

Cesenatico holds the Annual "Marco Pantani Nove Colli" cycling road event across nine of the Apennine foothills in May of each year. Other events associated include the Nove Colli Off Road and Junior Event in September each year.
